q: The basis of taxation is:
choices: Necessity, since government cannot exist without revenue, and the reciprocal duty of protection and support (benefits-protection theory)
hints: Taxes are the lifeblood of government.
Citizens receive protection and benefits in return.
why: Taxation rests on necessity (government cannot exist without funds) and on the benefits-protection theory: the State gives protection and benefits, and the people give support through taxes (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988

q: A taxpayer argues that he should not pay income tax because he receives no direct benefit from the government: he uses private schools, private hospitals and a private security agency. Is his argument valid?

alac.answer: No, his argument is not valid.
alac.basis: Taxation is an inherent power of the State, based on necessity and on the benefits-protection theory. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988, the Supreme Court described taxes as the lifeblood of the government, required for the protection and benefits the State gives to all. A tax is not a debt or a payment for a specific service, and the benefits received need not be direct or measured against the tax paid.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer enjoys the general benefits of organized government: peace and order, courts, laws that protect his property and contracts, and public infrastructure. That he chooses private services does not exempt him, because taxes are not based on the specific benefits each person receives.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he must pay income tax regardless of whether he personally uses particular public services.

keyPoints: Inherent power based on necessity
Benefits-protection theory
Tax is not a payment for specific services
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988

q: Which of the following is a constitutional limitation on the power of taxation under Article VI, Section 28(1) of the 1987 Constitution?
choices: Taxes may be collected only once every ten years
Taxes must be paid in gold
The rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable
hints: Inherent limitations include public purpose, territoriality and international comity.
Constitutional limitations are written in the Constitution.
why: 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 28(1): the rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. Other constitutional limitations include due process, equal protection, non-imprisonment for non-payment of poll tax, origination of revenue bills in the House, and exemptions of charitable and religious property.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 28

q: A city imposed a tax on all lands of a church, including (a) the chapel and convent used for worship and (b) a vacant lot that the church leases to a parking business. The church claims full exemption under the Constitution. Decide.

alac.answer: The chapel and convent are exempt, but the leased vacant lot is taxable.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 28(3) of the 1987 Constitution provides that charitable institutions, churches and personages or convents appurtenant thereto, mosques, non-profit cemeteries, and all lands, buildings, and improvements, actually, directly, and exclusively used for religious, charitable, or educational purposes shall be exempt from taxation. The exemption depends on the actual, direct and exclusive use of the property, not merely on the identity of the owner.
alac.application: Here, the chapel and convent are actually, directly and exclusively used for religious purposes, so they are exempt. The vacant lot is leased to a parking business; it is used for commercial purposes, not religious ones, even if the rent goes to the church.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the chapel and convent are exempt from the real property tax, while the leased lot may be taxed.

keyPoints: Exemption of property used for religious purposes (Art. VI, Sec. 28(3))
Test: actual, direct and exclusive use
Commercial use of church property is taxable
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 28(3)

q: Which of the following is a requisite of a valid tax?
choices: It must be payable in kind
It must be for a public purpose
It must be approved by a plebiscite
It must be imposed only on the rich
hints: The requisites are: public purpose, uniformity, within jurisdiction, and no violation of constitutional limits.
Public purpose is also an inherent limitation.
why: A valid tax must be (1) for a public purpose, (2) uniform, (3) within the jurisdiction of the taxing authority, and (4) not in violation of constitutional and inherent limitations, including due process (Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960).
cite: Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960

q: Congress passed a law imposing a special tax on all coconut farmers, the proceeds to be used to build a private road leading only to the vacation house of a senator. Is the tax valid?

alac.answer: No, the tax is not valid because it is not for a public purpose.
alac.basis: Taxes must be levied for a public purpose, which is both an inherent limitation and a requisite of a valid tax. In Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960, the Supreme Court struck down an appropriation of public funds for roads on private land, holding that public revenues may be used only for public purposes, and that the validity of a tax or appropriation depends on whether it benefits the public, not a private person.
alac.application: Here, the proceeds of the tax will be used to build a private road leading only to a senator's vacation house. That benefits a private individual, not the public.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the tax violates the public purpose requirement and is invalid.

keyPoints: Requisites of a valid tax: public purpose, uniformity, jurisdiction, constitutional limits
Public purpose as an inherent limitation
Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works
cite: Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960

q: Under the lifeblood doctrine, as stated in Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc.:
choices: The government may never compromise taxes
Taxes should be collected without unnecessary hindrance, but collection must be made in accordance with law
Taxpayers may refuse to pay while a case is pending
hints: Taxes are the lifeblood of government.
But the power must be exercised reasonably and lawfully.
why: Taxes are the lifeblood of the government and should be collected without unnecessary hindrance; but the collection must be made in accordance with law, as arbitrariness defeats the purpose (CIR v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988). This is why injunctions against tax collection are generally not allowed (NIRC Sec. 218).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988; National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 218

q: A corporation received a deficiency tax assessment and filed a case in the Regional Trial Court asking for an injunction to stop the BIR from collecting, arguing that the assessment is wrong. Should the RTC issue the injunction?

alac.answer: No, the RTC should not issue the injunction.
alac.basis: Under the lifeblood doctrine, taxes should be collected without unnecessary hindrance (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988). Section 218 of the NIRC provides that no court shall have the authority to grant an injunction to restrain the collection of any national internal revenue tax. The taxpayer's remedy is to protest the assessment and appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals, which alone may suspend collection under the conditions of its charter.
alac.application: Here, the corporation asked the RTC to enjoin the collection of a national internal revenue tax. The RTC has no authority to do so, regardless of whether the assessment is wrong.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the RTC should deny the injunction; the corporation should protest the assessment and, if necessary, seek relief from the CTA.

keyPoints: Lifeblood doctrine (CIR v. Algue)
No injunction to restrain collection of national taxes (Sec. 218)
Remedy: protest and appeal to the CTA
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc., G.R. No. L-28896, February 17, 1988; National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 218

q: In the construction of tax laws:
choices: Tax laws imposing taxes are construed strictly against the government, while tax exemptions are construed strictly against the taxpayer
Courts may extend tax laws by analogy
Tax exemptions are construed liberally in favor of the taxpayer
Tax laws are construed strictly against the taxpayer
hints: Doubt in a tax imposition favors the taxpayer.
Doubt in an exemption favors the government.
why: Tax laws are construed strictissimi juris against the government and liberally in favor of the taxpayer; tax exemptions are construed strictly against the taxpayer claiming them (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fortune Tobacco Corporation, G.R. Nos. 167274-75, July 21, 2008).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fortune Tobacco Corporation, G.R. Nos. 167274-75, July 21, 2008

q: A law grants a tax exemption to "cooperatives engaged in farming." A cooperative engaged in selling farm equipment, but not in farming, claims the exemption. Separately, a provision imposing a tax on "cigarettes" is unclear whether it covers heated tobacco sticks. How should each provision be construed?

alac.answer: The exemption should be denied to the equipment cooperative, and the unclear tax provision should be construed in favor of the taxpayer.
alac.basis: In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fortune Tobacco Corporation, G.R. Nos. 167274-75, July 21, 2008, the Supreme Court reiterated that tax laws are construed strictly against the government and liberally in favor of the taxpayer, so that a tax cannot be imposed without clear and express words; on the other hand, tax exemptions are construed strictissimi juris against the taxpayer, who must show a clear grant.
alac.application: Here, the exemption covers only cooperatives engaged in farming. The cooperative sells farm equipment; it does not farm, so it cannot claim an exemption that does not clearly cover it. As for the cigarette tax, if the law is truly unclear whether heated tobacco sticks are covered, the doubt is resolved in favor of the taxpayer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the equipment cooperative is not exempt, and the cigarette tax cannot be applied to heated tobacco sticks without clear words in the law.

keyPoints: Tax laws construed strictly against the government
Exemptions construed strictly against the taxpayer
CIR v. Fortune Tobacco
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fortune Tobacco Corporation, G.R. Nos. 167274-75, July 21, 2008

q: As a rule, may a taxpayer set off his tax liability against a claim he has against the government?
choices: Only if the claim is larger
No; taxes are not debts and cannot be the subject of set-off or compensation
hints: Taxes are not contracts but obligations created by law.
The lifeblood doctrine supports the rule.
why: Taxes cannot be subject to compensation or set-off, because the government and the taxpayer are not mutual creditors and debtors, and taxes are not debts (Philex Mining Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 125704, August 28, 1998; Francia v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-67649, June 28, 1988).
cite: Philex Mining Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 125704, August 28, 1998

q: A mining company owed P100 million in excise taxes. It refused to pay, claiming that the BIR owes it P120 million in pending VAT refunds, so the taxes should be set off. Is the set-off allowed?

alac.answer: No, the set-off is not allowed.
alac.basis: In Philex Mining Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 125704, August 28, 1998, the Supreme Court held that taxes cannot be the subject of compensation, because the government and the taxpayer are not creditors and debtors of each other; taxes are not debts but are due by law, and the collection of taxes cannot await the results of a lawsuit or a pending refund. A claim for refund that has not been granted is not a due, liquidated and demandable debt.
alac.application: Here, the mining company's excise taxes are due by law. Its pending VAT refunds are not yet granted or liquidated, and in any case taxes cannot be compensated against claims against the government.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company must pay the excise taxes and pursue its VAT refund separately.

keyPoints: No set-off or compensation of taxes
Taxes are not debts; the parties are not mutual creditors
Pending refunds are not liquidated and demandable
cite: Philex Mining Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 125704, August 28, 1998

q: Is double taxation prohibited by the 1987 Constitution?
choices: No; there is no constitutional prohibition against double taxation, though direct duplicate taxation may violate equal protection or uniformity
hints: Double taxation in the strict sense means taxing the same property twice, by the same authority, for the same purpose and period.
It is not forbidden as such.
why: There is no constitutional prohibition against double taxation in the Philippines; it is objectionable only if it violates equal protection or uniformity (Villanueva v. City of Iloilo, G.R. No. L-26521, December 28, 1968). Direct double taxation means the same property is taxed twice by the same taxing authority, for the same purpose, period and kind of tax.
cite: Villanueva v. City of Iloilo, G.R. No. L-26521, December 28, 1968

q: A city imposes a business tax on a store owner based on gross sales, and the national government imposes income tax on the same store's net income. The owner claims double taxation. Is the claim valid?

alac.answer: No, the claim is not valid; this is not prohibited double taxation.
alac.basis: In Villanueva v. City of Iloilo, G.R. No. L-26521, December 28, 1968, the Supreme Court held that there is no constitutional prohibition against double taxation, and that double taxation in the objectionable sense means taxing the same property twice by the same taxing authority, for the same purpose, during the same period, and with the same kind of tax. Different taxing authorities may tax the same subject in different ways.
alac.application: Here, the business tax is imposed by the city on the privilege of doing business, measured by gross sales, while the income tax is imposed by the national government on net income. The taxing authorities, the kinds of tax, and their purposes differ.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, there is no prohibited double taxation, and both taxes are valid.

keyPoints: No constitutional prohibition against double taxation
Direct double taxation: same authority, purpose, period and kind
Different authorities and kinds of tax (Villanueva v. City of Iloilo)
cite: Villanueva v. City of Iloilo, G.R. No. L-26521, December 28, 1968

q: In an indirect tax such as VAT, who may claim a refund of the tax under the rule in Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue?
choices: The statutory taxpayer, who is liable to pay the tax to the government
The final consumer who bore the tax
hints: The burden may be shifted, but the liability is not.
The buyer pays part of the price, not the tax.
why: In indirect taxes, the burden is shifted to the buyer, but the statutory taxpayer remains liable; only the statutory taxpayer may claim a refund (Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008).
cite: Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008

q: An airline bought aviation fuel from an oil company, which paid the excise tax to the BIR and passed it on to the airline in the price. The airline, claiming a tax exemption, filed a claim for refund of the excise tax. Will its claim prosper?

alac.answer: No, the airline's claim will not prosper; it is not the proper party to claim the refund.
alac.basis: In Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008, the Supreme Court held that excise taxes on petroleum products are indirect taxes whose liability falls on the manufacturer or seller, the statutory taxpayer, even though the burden is shifted to the buyer. The buyer pays the shifted tax as part of the price, not as a tax, and only the statutory taxpayer may file a claim for refund.
alac.application: Here, the oil company was the statutory taxpayer that paid the excise tax to the BIR. The airline only bore the economic burden of the tax as part of the price of the fuel.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the airline cannot claim the refund; at most, the oil company, as the statutory taxpayer, may claim it if the sale was exempt.

keyPoints: Shifting of the burden in indirect taxes
Statutory taxpayer remains liable
Only the statutory taxpayer may claim a refund (Silkair v. CIR)
cite: Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008

q: According to Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. The Estate of Benigno P. Toda, Jr., tax avoidance differs from tax evasion in that:
choices: Tax avoidance uses legal means to minimize taxes, while tax evasion uses illegal or fraudulent means
hints: Avoidance is tax planning; evasion is tax dodging.
Evasion requires a course of action that is unlawful, with intent.
why: Tax avoidance is the use of legally permissible means to reduce taxes; tax evasion is the use of illegal means to escape taxes, requiring (1) an end to pay less than the tax due, (2) an accompanying state of mind described as evil or in bad faith, and (3) a course of action that is unlawful (CIR v. Estate of Benigno P. Toda, Jr., G.R. No. 147188, September 14, 2004).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. The Estate of Benigno P. Toda, Jr., G.R. No. 147188, September 14, 2004

q: A corporation sold a building to a buyer for P200 million. To reduce taxes, it was made to appear that the building was first sold to an individual for P100 million, who resold it to the buyer the next day for P200 million, so the corporation would pay tax on a lower gain. The intermediary was a mere conduit. Is this tax avoidance or tax evasion?

alac.answer: This is tax evasion.
alac.basis: In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. The Estate of Benigno P. Toda, Jr., G.R. No. 147188, September 14, 2004, the Supreme Court distinguished tax avoidance, the use of legal means to minimize taxes, from tax evasion, which connotes the integration of three factors: (1) the end to be achieved, the payment of less than that known by the taxpayer to be legally due; (2) an accompanying state of mind described as evil, in bad faith, willful, or deliberate; and (3) a course of action or failure of action that is unlawful. The Court held that a sham two-step sale through a conduit, made to reduce the corporate income tax, was tax evasion.
alac.application: Here, the corporation interposed an individual who was a mere conduit, so that the real sale for P200 million would appear as a sale for P100 million. The aim was to pay less than the tax legally due, the scheme was deliberate, and the simulated sale was an unlawful course of action.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the scheme is tax evasion, and the corporation may be assessed on the true gain, with the fraud penalties and a ten-year period for assessment.

keyPoints: Avoidance: legal means; evasion: illegal means
Three elements of evasion (CIR v. Estate of Toda)
Sham sale through a conduit
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. The Estate of Benigno P. Toda, Jr., G.R. No. 147188, September 14, 2004

q: Under Section 204(A) of the NIRC, the Commissioner may compromise the payment of any internal revenue tax when:
choices: A reasonable doubt as to the validity of the claim against the taxpayer exists, or the financial position of the taxpayer demonstrates a clear inability to pay
The tax is above P1 million
hints: Compromise is a mutual concession.
Amnesty is a general pardon granted by law.
why: NIRC Sec. 204(A): the CIR may compromise when there is reasonable doubt as to the validity of the assessment, or the taxpayer's financial position shows clear inability to pay, subject to minimum compromise rates. A tax amnesty is a general pardon given by law, construed strictly against the taxpayer (CIR v. Marubeni Corporation, G.R. No. 137377, December 18, 2001).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 204; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Marubeni Corporation, G.R. No. 137377, December 18, 2001

q: A tax amnesty law excludes from its coverage "withholding agents with respect to their withholding tax liabilities." A corporation that availed of the amnesty argues that its deficiency withholding taxes are covered, since the law should be liberally construed. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, the corporation is not correct; its withholding tax liabilities are excluded.
alac.basis: A tax amnesty is a general pardon or intentional overlooking by the State of its authority to impose penalties on persons otherwise guilty of violations of tax laws. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Marubeni Corporation, G.R. No. 137377, December 18, 2001, the Supreme Court held that a tax amnesty, much like a tax exemption, is never favored nor presumed in law, and is construed strictly against the taxpayer, who must show complete compliance with the law.
alac.application: Here, the amnesty law expressly excludes withholding agents with respect to their withholding tax liabilities. Construed strictly against the taxpayer, the exclusion covers the corporation's deficiency withholding taxes, even if it validly availed of the amnesty for its other taxes.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation remains liable for its deficiency withholding taxes.

keyPoints: Tax amnesty is a general pardon
Construed strictly against the taxpayer (CIR v. Marubeni)
Express exclusions apply
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Marubeni Corporation, G.R. No. 137377, December 18, 2001

q: A taxpayer's suit may be filed to challenge:
choices: The illegal disbursement of public funds raised by taxation, or the use of public funds for an unconstitutional law
hints: The taxpayer must show a stake in the use of public funds.
Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works is the classic case.
why: A taxpayer may sue when public funds derived from taxation are disbursed in violation of law or of the Constitution; the taxpayer has an interest in preventing the illegal expenditure of public money (Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960).
cite: Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960

q: A citizen filed a suit to stop the release of P50 million from the national budget to a foundation privately owned by a mayor, arguing that the release violates the public purpose rule. The government argues that the citizen has no standing because he suffers no personal injury. Does he have standing?

alac.answer: Yes, the citizen has standing to file a taxpayer's suit.
alac.basis: In Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960, the Supreme Court recognized the standing of a taxpayer to question the validity of an appropriation and disbursement of public funds, because taxpayers have sufficient interest in preventing the illegal expenditure of moneys raised by taxation. The suit requires that public funds derived from taxation are being disbursed or are about to be disbursed in violation of law.
alac.application: Here, P50 million in public funds will be released to a private foundation owned by a mayor, allegedly for a private purpose. The citizen, as a taxpayer, has an interest in preventing the illegal use of public money even without a personal injury distinct from that of other taxpayers.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the citizen may file a taxpayer's suit to stop the release of the funds.

keyPoints: Taxpayer's suit to prevent illegal disbursement of public funds
Funds derived from taxation
Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works
cite: Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works and Communications, G.R. No. L-10405, December 29, 1960

q: Under Section 4 of the NIRC, the power to interpret the provisions of the Tax Code is under the exclusive and original jurisdiction of:
choices: The Commissioner of Internal Revenue, subject to review by the Secretary of Finance
hints: The Secretary of Finance promulgates rules upon the CIR's recommendation (Sec. 244).
The CIR cannot add requirements not in the law.
why: NIRC Sec. 4: the CIR has exclusive and original jurisdiction to interpret the Code, subject to review by the Secretary of Finance; the CIR decides disputed assessments and refunds, subject to the CTA's exclusive appellate jurisdiction. Congress alone may impose taxes. An administrative issuance cannot add to the law (CIR v. Michel J. Lhuillier Pawnshop, Inc., G.R. No. 150947, July 15, 2003).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 4; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Michel J. Lhuillier Pawnshop, Inc., G.R. No. 150947, July 15, 2003

q: The CIR issued a Revenue Memorandum Order declaring that pawnshops are subject to a tax that no law expressly imposes on them, reasoning that pawnshops are similar to lending investors. Is the order valid?

alac.answer: No, the order is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 4 of the NIRC gives the CIR the power to interpret tax laws, subject to review by the Secretary of Finance, and the Secretary of Finance promulgates rules for the Code's implementation. But the power to impose taxes belongs to Congress. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Michel J. Lhuillier Pawnshop, Inc., G.R. No. 150947, July 15, 2003, the Supreme Court invalidated a Revenue Memorandum Order that subjected pawnshops to a tax by treating them as lending investors, holding that the CIR cannot, by administrative issuance, impose a tax that the law does not.
alac.application: Here, the CIR's order imposes a tax on pawnshops by analogy, although no law imposes it on them. That is not interpretation but legislation, which the CIR has no power to do.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Revenue Memorandum Order is invalid.

keyPoints: CIR's power to interpret, subject to review (Sec. 4)
Power to impose taxes belongs to Congress
Administrative issuances cannot add taxes (CIR v. Michel J. Lhuillier Pawnshop)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 4; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Michel J. Lhuillier Pawnshop, Inc., G.R. No. 150947, July 15, 2003

q: Under Section 23 of the NIRC, a resident citizen is taxable on:
choices: Income from sources within the Philippines only
All income derived from sources within and without the Philippines
hints: The criteria are citizenship, residence and source of income.
Nonresident citizens and OFWs are taxed only on Philippine-source income.
why: NIRC Sec. 23(A): a resident citizen is taxable on all income from sources within and without the Philippines; Sec. 23(B)-(C): nonresident citizens and overseas contract workers are taxable only on income from Philippine sources; aliens and foreign corporations are taxed on Philippine-source income.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 23

q: Rosa, a Filipino nurse, works in Saudi Arabia under a two-year contract as an overseas contract worker. She earns her salary there and also receives rent from a condominium unit in Makati. Which of her incomes are subject to Philippine income tax?

alac.answer: Only her Makati rental income is subject to Philippine income tax; her Saudi salary is not.
alac.basis: Section 23(C) of the NIRC provides that an individual citizen of the Philippines who is working and deriving income from abroad as an overseas contract worker is taxable only on income derived from sources within the Philippines. Section 42(A) treats rentals from property located in the Philippines as income from sources within the Philippines.
alac.application: Here, Rosa is an overseas contract worker, so she is taxed only on Philippine-source income. Her salary is earned in Saudi Arabia, a foreign source. The rent from her Makati condominium comes from property located in the Philippines, a Philippine source.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rosa pays Philippine income tax only on her Makati rental income.

keyPoints: Criteria: citizenship, residence and source (Sec. 23)
Overseas contract workers taxed only on Philippine-source income (Sec. 23(C))
Rent from Philippine property is Philippine-source income (Sec. 42)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 23 and 42

q: Under Section 22(B) of the NIRC, which of the following is NOT treated as a corporation for income tax purposes?
hints: Business partnerships are taxed as corporations.
GPPs are pass-through entities; the partners pay the tax.
why: NIRC Sec. 22(B): the term corporation includes partnerships, joint-stock companies, joint accounts, associations and insurance companies, but not general professional partnerships and certain joint ventures or consortia; partners of a GPP are taxed on their distributive shares.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 22 and 26

q: Three lawyers formed a law partnership solely to practice law. Separately, three engineers formed a partnership to sell construction materials. How are the two partnerships treated for income tax purposes?

alac.answer: The law partnership is a general professional partnership not taxed as a corporation; the engineers' partnership is taxed as a corporation.
alac.basis: Section 22(B) of the NIRC provides that the term corporation includes partnerships, no matter how created or organized, but does not include general professional partnerships, which are partnerships formed by persons for the sole purpose of exercising their common profession, no part of the income of which is derived from engaging in any trade or business. Under Section 26, a general professional partnership is not subject to income tax, but its partners are liable for tax in their individual capacities on their distributive shares.
alac.application: Here, the lawyers formed a partnership solely to practice their common profession, so it is a general professional partnership. The engineers' partnership sells construction materials, which is a trade or business, so it is taxed as a corporation even though its partners are professionals.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the lawyers pay tax individually on their shares, while the engineers' partnership itself pays corporate income tax.

keyPoints: Partnerships generally taxed as corporations (Sec. 22(B))
General professional partnership: sole purpose of exercising a common profession
Partners of a GPP taxed on distributive shares (Sec. 26)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 22 and 26

q: In Madrigal v. Rafferty, the Supreme Court distinguished income from capital by describing:
choices: Capital as a fund and income as a flow of services or wealth over a period of time
Income as a fund and capital as a flow
Income as property owned at a point in time
hints: Capital is wealth at an instant.
Income is the gain derived from capital over time.
why: Income is the amount of money coming to a person within a specified time, a flow of services rendered by capital; capital is a fund, wealth existing at a point in time (Madrigal v. Rafferty, G.R. No. L-12287, August 7, 1918). NIRC Sec. 32(A): gross income means all income derived from whatever source.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 32; Madrigal v. Rafferty, G.R. No. L-12287, August 7, 1918

q: Sonny received P5 million from an insurance company as indemnity for his house destroyed by fire, the house having cost him P5 million. He also received P1 million as interest on his savings. Which of these is income?

alac.answer: The P1 million interest is income; the P5 million fire indemnity is a return of capital, not income.
alac.basis: In Madrigal v. Rafferty, G.R. No. L-12287, August 7, 1918, the Supreme Court explained that capital is a fund and income is a flow; income is the gain derived from capital, labor, or both. Section 32(A) of the NIRC defines gross income as all income derived from whatever source, including interests. A recovery that merely restores lost capital, without gain, is not income.
alac.application: Here, the P5 million indemnity only replaced the P5 million value of the destroyed house, so Sonny gained nothing; it is a return of capital. The P1 million interest is a gain derived from his capital, his savings, and is expressly included in gross income.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, only the interest is income subject to tax.

keyPoints: Capital is a fund; income is a flow (Madrigal v. Rafferty)
Gross income includes interests (Sec. 32(A))
Return of capital without gain is not income
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 32; Madrigal v. Rafferty, G.R. No. L-12287, August 7, 1918

q: As a general rule, are stock dividends income to the shareholder?
choices: No, because they merely represent a transfer of surplus to capital; but their later redemption or cancellation may be taxable
hints: Income must be realized.
Redemption of stock dividends can be treated as a taxable dividend.
why: Stock dividends are not income because the shareholder's proportionate interest is unchanged and nothing is realized; but the redemption or cancellation of stock dividends in a manner essentially equivalent to a taxable dividend is taxable (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and A. Soriano Corp., G.R. No. 108576, January 20, 1999).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and A. Soriano Corp., G.R. No. 108576, January 20, 1999

q: A corporation declared stock dividends to its sole foreign shareholder, who received new shares. Years later, the corporation redeemed those same shares for cash, without any business purpose other than to distribute its earnings. Is the shareholder taxable, and when?

alac.answer: The shareholder is not taxable on the stock dividends when received, but the redemption is taxable as a dividend.
alac.basis: As a rule, stock dividends are not income, because the shareholder's proportional interest in the corporation is unchanged and no gain is realized. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and A. Soriano Corp., G.R. No. 108576, January 20, 1999, the Supreme Court held that the redemption or cancellation of stock dividends, depending on the time and manner it is made, may be essentially equivalent to the distribution of taxable dividends, and is then taxable; income is realized when the shareholder receives cash for the shares.
alac.application: Here, the receipt of the stock dividends did not change the shareholder's interest or give it any realized gain. But the later redemption of those same shares for cash, without a business purpose other than distributing earnings, is essentially equivalent to a cash dividend; the shareholder then realized income.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the shareholder is taxable at the time of the redemption, and the corporation must withhold the corresponding tax.

keyPoints: Income must be realized
Stock dividends generally not income
Redemption essentially equivalent to a dividend is taxable (CIR v. CA and A. Soriano Corp.)
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals and A. Soriano Corp., G.R. No. 108576, January 20, 1999

q: Under Section 32(B)(1) of the NIRC, the proceeds of life insurance paid to the beneficiaries upon the death of the insured are:
choices: Taxable only if above P1 million
Excluded from gross income, but interest paid by the insurer on amounts held is included
hints: Exclusions are not part of gross income at all.
Interest earned on the proceeds is different.
why: NIRC Sec. 32(B)(1): proceeds of life insurance paid to heirs or beneficiaries upon the death of the insured are excluded from gross income, but interest on amounts held by the insurer is included. Sec. 32(B) lists other exclusions (return of premiums, gifts and inheritances, compensation for injuries, retirement benefits, etc.).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 32(B)

q: Upon Tomas's death, his insurer paid his wife P3 million as beneficiary of his life policy. At her request, the insurer kept the P3 million and paid her P150,000 in interest a year. She also received P500,000 in moral damages in a suit for injuries she suffered in a car accident. Which of these must she report as gross income?

alac.answer: Only the P150,000 annual interest must be included in gross income.
alac.basis: Section 32(B)(1) of the NIRC excludes from gross income the proceeds of life insurance policies paid to the heirs or beneficiaries upon the death of the insured, but if such amounts are held by the insurer under an agreement to pay interest thereon, the interest payments shall be included in gross income. Section 32(B)(4) excludes amounts received as compensation for personal injuries or sickness, plus the amount of damages received on account of such injuries.
alac.application: Here, the P3 million life insurance proceeds are excluded. The P150,000 a year is interest on proceeds held by the insurer under an agreement, so it is included. The P500,000 moral damages compensate her personal injuries in the accident, so they are excluded.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she must report only the annual interest as gross income.

keyPoints: Life insurance proceeds excluded (Sec. 32(B)(1))
Interest on proceeds held by the insurer included
Damages for personal injuries excluded (Sec. 32(B)(4))
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 32(B)

q: Under Section 32(A)(1) of the NIRC, compensation income includes:
choices: Compensation for services in whatever form paid, including fees, salaries, wages, commissions and similar items
hints: The form of payment does not matter.
Benefits in kind may be compensation.
why: NIRC Sec. 32(A)(1): gross income includes compensation for services in whatever form paid, including fees, salaries, wages, commissions and similar items; employees earning purely compensation income are not allowed itemized deductions (Sec. 34, introductory paragraph).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 32 and 34

q: Vic, a rank-and-file employee, receives a monthly salary, sales commissions, and a car given by his employer as a reward for meeting his sales target. He also wants to deduct his commuting expenses from his salary. Which items are compensation income, and may he deduct his commuting expenses?

alac.answer: His salary, commissions and the car are all compensation income, and he may not deduct his commuting expenses.
alac.basis: Section 32(A)(1) of the NIRC includes in gross income compensation for services in whatever form paid, including fees, salaries, wages, commissions, and similar items. Section 34 provides that taxpayers earning compensation income arising from personal services rendered under an employer-employee relationship shall not be allowed deductions under that section, other than those under subsection (M).
alac.application: Here, Vic's salary and commissions are compensation for his services. The car, though not cash, was given for meeting his sales target, so it is compensation in kind, valued at its fair market value. As a purely compensation income earner, Vic may not claim itemized deductions such as commuting expenses.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, all three items are compensation income, and his commuting expenses are not deductible.

keyPoints: Compensation in whatever form paid (Sec. 32(A)(1))
Benefits in kind are compensation
No itemized deductions for pure compensation earners (Sec. 34)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 32 and 34

q: Under Section 34(L) of the NIRC, as amended by RA 9504, an individual earning professional or business income may elect an optional standard deduction (OSD) of not more than:
choices: 40% of gross sales or gross receipts
hints: RA 9504 increased the OSD.
The election is irrevocable for the taxable year.
why: NIRC Sec. 34(L), as amended by RA 9504: an individual (other than a nonresident alien) may elect an OSD not exceeding 40% of gross sales or gross receipts; corporations may elect 40% of gross income. Professional income, such as fees of lawyers and doctors, may be subject to the OSD or to itemized deductions.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 34(L), as amended by RA 9504

q: Dr. Wena, a self-employed doctor, earned professional fees of P3 million. Her actual expenses were only P600,000, and she kept few receipts. She asks which deduction method is better for her and whether she can switch methods after filing her return. Advise her.

alac.answer: The optional standard deduction is better for her, but once elected in her return it is irrevocable for that taxable year.
alac.basis: Section 34(L) of the NIRC, as amended by RA 9504, provides that an individual subject to tax under Section 24, other than a nonresident alien, may elect a standard deduction in an amount not exceeding forty percent of his gross sales or gross receipts, in lieu of itemized deductions, and that such election, when made in the return, shall be irrevocable for the taxable year. Professional fees are income from the exercise of a profession under Section 32(A)(2).
alac.application: Here, the OSD of 40% of P3 million is P1.2 million, double her actual expenses of P600,000, and she need not prove the expenses with receipts. But she must elect it in her return, and she cannot change her choice for that year after filing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she should elect the OSD in her return, knowing that the election is irrevocable for that year (and she may instead consider the 8% option if qualified).

keyPoints: Professional income (Sec. 32(A)(2))
OSD of 40% of gross receipts (Sec. 34(L), as amended by RA 9504)
Election irrevocable for the taxable year
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 32 and 34(L), as amended by RA 9504

q: Passive income, such as interest on bank deposits and royalties, is generally:
choices: Subject to the graduated income tax rates together with business income
Subject to final withholding tax at source, and not included in the taxable income subject to graduated rates
hints: Active income comes from the conduct of business or a profession.
Passive income is earned without active involvement and is usually taxed finally at source.
why: Active income (from business, profession or employment) is taxed at graduated or regular rates on net income; passive income such as interest, royalties, prizes and dividends is generally subject to final tax withheld at source under NIRC Secs. 24(B), 25, 27(D) and 28, as amended.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 24(B) and 57

q: A bank paid Xiao interest on her savings deposit and withheld the final tax. Xiao, who also runs a bakery, wants to include the interest in her bakery's taxable income and deduct her bakery expenses from it. Separately, she wants to treat her bakery profits as passive income. Is either proper?

alac.answer: Neither is proper.
alac.basis: Under the NIRC, as amended, interest on bank deposits is passive income subject to a final tax withheld at source by the bank (Secs. 24(B) and 57(A)). Income subject to final tax is not included in the taxable income subject to the graduated rates, and no deductions are allowed against it. Business income, by contrast, is active income derived from the conduct of trade or business, subject to the regular income tax on taxable income after allowable deductions (Sec. 32(A)(2)).
alac.application: Here, the bank already withheld the final tax on Xiao's interest, so that income is fully taxed and cannot be combined with her bakery income or reduced by bakery expenses. Her bakery profits come from her active conduct of business, so they are active income, not passive income.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the interest stays under the final tax, and the bakery income is taxed as business income on its net amount.

keyPoints: Passive income generally subject to final tax at source
No deductions against income subject to final tax
Business income is active income taxed on net income
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 24(B), 32 and 57

q: Under Section 39(A)(1) of the NIRC, which of the following is a capital asset?
choices: A residential house owned by an employee and not used in any business
Stock in trade of the taxpayer
Depreciable property used in the business
Property held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business
hints: Capital assets are defined by exclusion.
Everything not listed as ordinary is a capital asset.
why: NIRC Sec. 39(A)(1): capital assets are property held by the taxpayer, whether or not connected with business, but excluding stock in trade, inventory, property held primarily for sale to customers, depreciable property used in business, and real property used in business. Inherited land subdivided and sold as a business becomes an ordinary asset (Calasanz v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. L-26284, October 9, 1986).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 39; Calasanz v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. L-26284, October 9, 1986

q: Yna inherited a large tract of land. She had it subdivided into 200 lots, built roads and drainage, advertised them, and sold the lots on installment over several years. She reported her gains as capital gains. The BIR assessed her for ordinary income tax. Who is correct?

alac.answer: The BIR is correct; the lots became ordinary assets.
alac.basis: Section 39(A)(1) of the NIRC defines capital assets as property held by the taxpayer, but excludes property held by the taxpayer primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of his trade or business. In Calasanz v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. L-26284, October 9, 1986, the Supreme Court held that inherited land, which the heirs subdivided, improved with roads, and sold in lots to the public, was converted from a capital asset into an ordinary asset, because the heirs engaged in the real estate business.
alac.application: Here, Yna did more than merely sell inherited land. She subdivided it into 200 lots, introduced improvements, advertised, and sold the lots on installment over several years. These acts show that she held the lots primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of a business.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the gains are ordinary income, and the BIR's assessment is correct.

keyPoints: Capital assets defined by exclusion (Sec. 39(A)(1))
Property held primarily for sale to customers is ordinary
Subdivision and sale of inherited land as a business (Calasanz v. CIR)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 39; Calasanz v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. L-26284, October 9, 1986

q: Under Section 42(A) of the NIRC, interest is treated as income from sources within the Philippines if it is:
choices: Derived from sources within the Philippines, including interest on bonds, notes or other interest-bearing obligations of residents
hints: The source of interest is the residence of the debtor.
Royalties are sourced where the property is used.
why: NIRC Sec. 42(A) lists Philippine-source income: interest on obligations of residents; dividends from domestic corporations (and some foreign ones); compensation for services performed in the Philippines; rentals and royalties from property located or used in the Philippines; and gains from sale of Philippine real property.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 42

q: Zack, a nonresident alien not engaged in business in the Philippines, (a) lent money to a Philippine resident corporation and received interest, paid into his bank account in Hong Kong; and (b) licensed a Philippine company to use his patent in its factory in Laguna and received royalties in Singapore. Are these incomes subject to Philippine income tax?

alac.answer: Yes, both are Philippine-source income subject to Philippine income tax.
alac.basis: Section 42(A) of the NIRC treats as income from sources within the Philippines (1) interests on bonds, notes or other interest-bearing obligations of residents, corporate or otherwise, and (4) rentals and royalties from property located in the Philippines or from any interest in such property, including the use of patents in the Philippines. Nonresident aliens are taxable on income from sources within the Philippines.
alac.application: Here, the interest comes from a loan to a Philippine resident corporation, so its source is the Philippines, regardless of where payment is made. The royalties are paid for the use of the patent in a factory in Laguna, so they are sourced in the Philippines, regardless of where they are received.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, both the interest and the royalties are subject to Philippine income tax, generally through final withholding by the Philippine payors.

keyPoints: Interest sourced at the residence of the debtor (Sec. 42(A)(1))
Royalties sourced where the property is used (Sec. 42(A)(4))
Place of payment does not matter
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 23 and 42

q: What is the difference between a tax deduction and a tax credit?
choices: A deduction is subtracted from the tax due; a credit reduces gross income
A deduction reduces gross income to arrive at taxable income; a credit is subtracted directly from the tax due
hints: Deductions are allowed under Sec. 34.
Example of a credit: foreign income taxes paid by a resident citizen.
why: Deductions (NIRC Sec. 34) are subtracted from gross income to arrive at taxable income, such as ordinary and necessary business expenses; tax credits are subtracted from the income tax due, such as foreign income taxes paid by resident citizens and domestic corporations (Sec. 34(C)(3)) and creditable withholding taxes.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 34

q: Abe, a resident citizen, has a business in Manila and a rental property in Japan, where he paid Japanese income tax on the rent. He paid salaries to his Manila staff. He asks how to treat the staff salaries and the Japanese income tax in his Philippine return. Advise him.

alac.answer: The staff salaries are deductions from gross income, while the Japanese income tax may be claimed as a tax credit, or alternatively as a deduction.
alac.basis: Section 34(A)(1)(a) of the NIRC allows as deduction from gross income all the ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred in carrying on the trade or business, including a reasonable allowance for salaries. Section 34(C)(3) allows resident citizens to credit against their Philippine income tax the income taxes paid to a foreign country, subject to limitations, or alternatively to deduct them. A deduction reduces taxable income, while a credit reduces the tax itself.
alac.application: Here, the staff salaries are ordinary and necessary business expenses, so they are deducted from Abe's gross income. As a resident citizen, he is taxed on his Japanese rent, but he may credit the Japanese income tax against his Philippine tax, subject to the limits, which is usually more beneficial than deducting it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Abe should deduct the salaries and claim the Japanese tax as a foreign tax credit.

keyPoints: Deductions reduce gross income (Sec. 34(A))
Tax credits reduce the tax due (Sec. 34(C)(3))
Foreign tax credit for resident citizens
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 34

q: Which of the following taxpayers may NOT elect the optional standard deduction under Section 34(L) of the NIRC, as amended?
choices: A resident citizen engaged in business
hints: The law expressly excludes one group.
Corporations may elect 40% of gross income.
why: NIRC Sec. 34(L), as amended by RA 9504: individuals subject to Sec. 24, other than nonresident aliens, may elect an OSD of up to 40% of gross sales or receipts; corporations subject to Secs. 27(A) and 28(A)(1) may elect 40% of gross income.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 34(L), as amended by RA 9504

q: Ben Corp., a domestic corporation, had gross sales of P10 million and cost of sales of P6 million, so its gross income was P4 million. Its itemized operating expenses were P1 million. It wants to elect the OSD. How much OSD may it claim, and is it better than itemizing?

alac.answer: Ben Corp. may claim an OSD of P1.6 million, which is better than its P1 million itemized expenses.
alac.basis: Section 34(L) of the NIRC, as amended by RA 9504, provides that a corporation subject to tax under Sections 27(A) and 28(A)(1) may elect a standard deduction in an amount not exceeding forty percent of its gross income, in lieu of itemized deductions. For corporations, gross income means gross sales less sales returns, discounts and allowances and cost of goods sold.
alac.application: Here, Ben Corp.'s gross income is P4 million (P10 million sales less P6 million cost of sales). Forty percent of P4 million is P1.6 million, which exceeds its itemized expenses of P1 million.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ben Corp. may elect an OSD of P1.6 million, which is more advantageous, and its election in the return is irrevocable for the year.

keyPoints: Corporations may elect OSD of 40% of gross income (Sec. 34(L))
Gross income for corporations: sales less cost of sales
Compare with itemized deductions
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 34(L), as amended by RA 9504

q: The rationale of the withholding tax system includes:
choices: Providing the taxpayer a convenient way of paying, ensuring collection of taxes, and improving the government's cash flow
Allowing payors to keep the taxes
hints: The payor collects the tax at source.
Taxes withheld are held in trust for the government.
why: The withholding system makes tax collection easier and more certain, gives taxpayers a convenient way to pay, and improves the government's cash flow; taxes withheld are held as a special fund in trust for the government until paid (NIRC Sec. 58(A); Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 57 and 58; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003

q: A company withheld taxes from its employees' salaries but used the money to pay its suppliers during a cash shortage, intending to remit it to the BIR later. Is the company's act justified?

alac.answer: No, the company's act is not justified.
alac.basis: The withholding tax system is designed to ensure the collection of taxes at source and the government's cash flow (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003). Section 58(A) of the NIRC provides that the taxes deducted and withheld by the withholding agent shall be held as a special fund in trust for the government until paid to the collecting officers. Section 251 penalizes any person required to withhold, account for and remit any tax who willfully fails to do so.
alac.application: Here, the withheld taxes were not the company's money; they were held in trust for the government. Using them to pay suppliers, even temporarily, is a breach of that trust and a failure to remit the taxes on time.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company is liable for the unremitted taxes with penalties, and its responsible officers may be held liable under Section 251.

keyPoints: Rationale of withholding: collection at source and cash flow
Withheld taxes held in trust for the government (Sec. 58(A))
Penalty for failure to remit (Sec. 251)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 58 and 251; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003

q: In a final withholding tax, as explained in Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation:
choices: The withholding agent is never liable
The payee still files a return and pays more tax
The tax may be credited against other income taxes
The amount withheld is the full and final tax on the income, and the payee need not report the income
hints: Creditable withholding is only an advance payment.
In final withholding, the agent's liability is direct.
why: In final withholding, the tax withheld is the full and final payment of the tax on the income; the payee no longer reports it, and the withholding agent is directly liable for the tax. In creditable withholding, the tax withheld is an advance payment, credited against the payee's income tax due (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003

q: A company paid professional fees to a consultant and withheld 10% as creditable withholding tax. It also paid royalties to a nonresident foreign company and withheld the final tax. At year-end, the consultant wants to treat the 10% as his full tax, and the foreign company asks whether it must file a Philippine return. Advise both.

alac.answer: The consultant must still report his fees and may only credit the 10% against his tax due; the foreign company need not file a return for the royalties.
alac.basis: Under the NIRC, as amended, and as explained in Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003, in creditable withholding the tax withheld is intended to equal or approximate the tax due on the income and is credited against the payee's income tax liability for the year; the payee must still report the income. In final withholding, the amount withheld is the full and final payment of the income tax due, the payee is not required to file a return for that income, and the liability for payment rests primarily on the withholding agent.
alac.application: Here, the 10% withheld from the consultant's fees is creditable, so it is only an advance payment; he must include the fees in his return and pay any balance, or claim any excess. The tax on the foreign company's royalties is final, so the foreign company has fully paid its Philippine tax on that income.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the consultant must file and settle his annual tax, while the foreign company has no further filing obligation for the royalties.

keyPoints: Creditable withholding: advance payment credited against tax due
Final withholding: full and final tax; no return for that income
CIR v. Solidbank
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Solidbank Corporation, G.R. No. 148191, November 25, 2003

q: Under Section 251 of the NIRC, a person required to withhold and remit any tax who willfully fails to do so is liable, upon conviction, to:
choices: A penalty equal to the total amount of the tax not withheld, or not accounted for and remitted, in addition to other penalties
hints: The withholding agent is personally liable.
Failure to refund excess withholding is also penalized (Sec. 252).
why: NIRC Sec. 251: a person required to withhold, account for and remit taxes who willfully fails to do so is liable, in addition to other penalties, to a penalty equal to the tax not withheld or not remitted; Sec. 252: employers failing to refund excess withholding are liable for the amount not refunded.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 251 and 252

q: Carla, the treasurer of a corporation, deliberately did not withhold taxes on the salaries of the corporation's executives, to make the executives happy. The BIR assessed the corporation for the deficiency withholding taxes and filed a criminal case. What are the liabilities of the corporation and of Carla?

alac.answer: The corporation is liable for the deficiency withholding taxes, and Carla may be held criminally liable with the penalty under Section 251.
alac.basis: Under the NIRC, the withholding agent is liable for the taxes it is required to withhold, which are held in trust for the government (Sec. 58). Section 251 provides that any person required to withhold, account for, and remit any tax who willfully fails to withhold such tax shall, in addition to other penalties, be liable upon conviction to a penalty equal to the total amount of the tax not withheld. For corporations, the penalty applies to the officers responsible for the violation (Sec. 253(d)).
alac.application: Here, the corporation, as withholding agent, failed to withhold taxes on its executives' salaries, so it is liable for the deficiency withholding taxes with interest and surcharges. Carla, as treasurer, willfully decided not to withhold, so she is the responsible officer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation must pay the deficiency taxes, and Carla may be convicted and made to pay a penalty equal to the taxes not withheld, in addition to other penalties.

keyPoints: Withholding agent liable for taxes required to be withheld
Willful failure to withhold penalized (Sec. 251)
Responsible corporate officers liable
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 58, 251 and 253

q: Under Section 105 of the NIRC, VAT is imposed on any person who:
choices: Sells goods only once as a private individual
In the course of trade or business, sells, barters, exchanges or leases goods or properties, or renders services, and any person who imports goods
hints: The key phrase is 'in the course of trade or business'.
Importers are subject to VAT even if not in business.
why: NIRC Sec. 105: VAT applies to sales, barters, exchanges or leases of goods or properties and sales of services in the course of trade or business, and to importations; 'in the course of trade or business' means the regular conduct or pursuit of a commercial or economic activity, even by non-stock, non-profit organizations or government entities.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 105

q: Dana, an employee, sold her personal car once to a friend. Separately, a non-stock, non-profit hospital regularly rents out spaces in its building to restaurants and shops. Are these transactions subject to VAT?

alac.answer: Dana's sale is not subject to VAT, but the hospital's regular rentals are.
alac.basis: Section 105 of the NIRC imposes VAT on any person who, in the course of trade or business, sells or leases goods or properties or renders services. It defines "in the course of trade or business" as the regular conduct or pursuit of a commercial or an economic activity, including transactions incidental thereto, by any person regardless of whether the person engaged therein is a non-stock, non-profit private organization or a government entity.
alac.application: Here, Dana's single sale of her personal car is an isolated transaction, not the regular pursuit of a commercial activity. The hospital, although non-stock and non-profit, regularly leases spaces to restaurants and shops, which is the regular conduct of a commercial activity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dana's sale is not subject to VAT, while the hospital's rentals are subject to VAT if they exceed the VAT threshold.

keyPoints: VAT on sales and leases in the course of trade or business (Sec. 105)
Regular conduct of a commercial or economic activity
Non-stock, non-profit status does not matter
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 105

q: In VAT, the impact of taxation falls on the seller, while the incidence of taxation falls on:
choices: The buyer or final consumer, to whom the tax is shifted
hints: VAT is an indirect tax (Sec. 105).
A VAT-exempt buyer cannot automatically refuse the passed-on VAT.
why: NIRC Sec. 105: VAT is an indirect tax that may be shifted to the buyer. Impact is on the statutory taxpayer (seller); incidence is on the buyer who bears the burden. A VAT exemption of the buyer does not exempt it from VAT passed on by a seller unless the law exempts the transaction (Contex Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 151135, July 2, 2004).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 105; Contex Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 151135, July 2, 2004

q: Ex Corp., a VAT-exempt enterprise in a special economic zone, bought supplies from a local VAT-registered seller, who passed on the 12% VAT in the price. Ex Corp. filed a claim with the BIR for refund of the VAT it paid, arguing that it is exempt from VAT. Will the claim prosper?

alac.answer: No, Ex Corp.'s claim will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 105 of the NIRC provides that VAT is an indirect tax whose amount may be shifted or passed on to the buyer. The seller is the statutory taxpayer (the impact of the tax), while the buyer bears the burden (the incidence). In Contex Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 151135, July 2, 2004, the Supreme Court held that a VAT-exempt buyer that paid the VAT passed on by its seller is not the proper party to claim a refund, because the VAT it paid was part of the purchase price, and the remedy is for the seller, as statutory taxpayer, to claim the refund or for the buyer to seek reimbursement from the seller.
alac.application: Here, the local seller is the statutory taxpayer that remitted the VAT. Ex Corp. merely bore the VAT as part of the price of the supplies. Its exemption from VAT does not make it the proper party to claim a refund from the BIR.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ex Corp.'s claim for refund will be denied; its remedy is against the seller, which may claim a refund if the sale was in fact zero-rated.

keyPoints: Impact on the seller; incidence on the buyer
VAT is an indirect tax (Sec. 105)
Buyer bearing passed-on VAT is not the proper party to claim refund (Contex v. CIR)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 105; Contex Corporation v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 151135, July 2, 2004

q: Under the destination principle in VAT:
choices: Goods and services are taxed only in the country where they are consumed; exports are zero-rated and imports are taxed
Goods are taxed in the country of production
hints: The Philippines follows the destination principle.
Under the cross-border doctrine, no VAT is due on goods consumed outside the Philippine customs territory.
why: Under the destination principle, goods and services are taxed only where consumed, so exports are zero-rated and imports are taxed. Under the cross-border doctrine, no VAT is imposed on goods destined for consumption outside the Philippine customs territory, including ecozones (Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Toshiba Information Equipment (Phils.), Inc., G.R. No. 150154, August 9, 2005).
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Toshiba Information Equipment (Phils.), Inc., G.R. No. 150154, August 9, 2005

q: A Manila-based manufacturer sold goods to an enterprise registered in a special economic zone, which is treated as a separate customs territory. The BIR assessed 12% VAT on the sale, arguing that the goods never left the Philippines physically. Is the assessment correct?

alac.answer: No, the sale is zero-rated, and the assessment is incorrect.
alac.basis: Under the destination principle, goods and services are taxed only in the country where they are consumed. Under the cross-border doctrine, no VAT shall be imposed on goods destined for consumption outside the territorial border of the taxing authority. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Toshiba Information Equipment (Phils.), Inc., G.R. No. 150154, August 9, 2005, the Supreme Court held that ecozones are treated as separate customs territories, so sales to ecozone enterprises are treated as exports and are zero-rated. The TRAIN law likewise lists as export sales the sale and delivery of goods to registered enterprises within a separate customs territory.
alac.application: Here, the buyer is registered in a special economic zone, a separate customs territory. Although the goods did not physically leave the Philippines, they are destined for consumption outside the Philippine customs territory, so the sale is treated as an export sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is subject to zero percent VAT, and the 12% VAT assessment should be cancelled.

keyPoints: Destination principle
Cross-border doctrine; ecozones as separate customs territories (CIR v. Toshiba)
Sales to ecozone enterprises are zero-rated export sales
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 106(A)(2), as amended by RA 10963; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Toshiba Information Equipment (Phils.), Inc., G.R. No. 150154, August 9, 2005

q: Under Section 106(B) of the NIRC, which of the following is a transaction deemed sale subject to VAT?
choices: A sale to a customer at a discount
Retirement from or cessation of business, with respect to inventories of taxable goods existing at that time
hints: Deemed sales tax goods that leave the VAT chain without an actual sale.
There are four kinds.
why: NIRC Sec. 106(B): deemed sales are (1) transfer, use or consumption not in the course of business of goods intended for sale or for business use; (2) distribution to shareholders or creditors; (3) consignment not sold within 60 days; and (4) retirement from or cessation of business, as to remaining inventories.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 106(B)

q: A VAT-registered appliance store (a) gave refrigerators from its inventory to its shareholders as their share in the profits, (b) gave one TV from its stock to the owner's daughter as a wedding gift, and (c) closed its business with P2 million in unsold appliances. Are these subject to VAT though no actual sale took place?

alac.answer: Yes, all three are transactions deemed sale subject to VAT.
alac.basis: Section 106(B) of the NIRC provides that the following transactions shall be deemed sale: (1) transfer, use or consumption not in the course of business of goods or properties originally intended for sale or for use in the course of business; (2) distribution or transfer to shareholders or investors as share in the profits of the VAT-registered persons, or to creditors in payment of debt; (3) consignment of goods if actual sale is not made within sixty days; and (4) retirement from or cessation of business, with respect to inventories of taxable goods existing as of such retirement or cessation.
alac.application: Here, (a) the refrigerators were distributed to shareholders as their share in the profits; (b) the TV from inventory intended for sale was transferred not in the course of business as a personal gift; and (c) the store ceased business with P2 million in taxable inventories.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the store must pay output VAT on all three, based on the market value or cost of the goods as the rules provide.

keyPoints: Transactions deemed sale (Sec. 106(B))
Distribution to shareholders; personal use of inventory
Cessation of business with inventories
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 106(B)

q: What is the main difference between a zero-rated sale and a VAT-exempt sale?
choices: An exempt sale allows input VAT refund
A zero-rated sale is subject to 12% VAT
In a zero-rated sale, the seller may claim a refund or credit of its input VAT; in an exempt sale, the seller cannot
hints: Both result in no output VAT.
Only zero-rating keeps the input tax creditable.
why: Zero-rated sales are taxable at 0%, so the seller may claim a refund or tax credit of input VAT attributable to them; exempt sales are outside the VAT system, so input VAT is not creditable and becomes part of cost. Export sales of goods (Sec. 106(A)(2), as amended by TRAIN) and services to nonresidents doing business outside the Philippines are zero-rated (Accenture, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 190102, July 11, 2012).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 106(A)(2) and 108(B), as amended; Accenture, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 190102, July 11, 2012

q: A Philippine IT company rendered software services to a foreign client and was paid in dollars. It claimed the sale is zero-rated and sought a refund of its input VAT. The BIR found that the foreign client was actually doing business in the Philippines through a local branch. Is the sale zero-rated?

alac.answer: No, the sale is not zero-rated, so the input VAT refund should be denied.
alac.basis: Section 108(B) of the NIRC, as amended, zero-rates services other than processing, manufacturing or repacking of goods rendered to a person engaged in business conducted outside the Philippines, paid for in acceptable foreign currency. In Accenture, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 190102, July 11, 2012, the Supreme Court held that, for services to be zero-rated, the recipient must be doing business outside the Philippines, and that payment in foreign currency alone is not enough. Only zero-rated sales allow the refund of attributable input VAT.
alac.application: Here, the IT company was paid in dollars, but the foreign client was doing business in the Philippines through a local branch. The recipient requirement is not met.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is subject to 12% VAT, not zero-rated, and there is no basis for the refund of input VAT as attributable to zero-rated sales.

keyPoints: Zero-rated services: recipient doing business outside the Philippines, paid in foreign currency (Sec. 108(B))
Payment in foreign currency alone is insufficient (Accenture v. CIR)
Only zero-rated sales allow input VAT refund
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 108(B), as amended; Accenture, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 190102, July 11, 2012

q: Under Section 109 of the NIRC, as amended, which of the following is VAT-exempt?
choices: Sale of agricultural and marine food products in their original state
Sale of appliances by a VAT-registered store
hints: Basic food in its original state is exempt.
Educational services of accredited private schools are exempt too.
why: NIRC Sec. 109(1), as amended, lists VAT-exempt transactions, including the sale or importation of agricultural and marine food products in their original state, educational services by accredited private educational institutions, and services rendered by individuals under an employer-employee relationship, among others.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 109, as amended

q: Edna, a VAT-registered farmer, sells (a) fresh unpeeled mangoes and (b) dried mangoes packed in sealed plastic for supermarkets. A private accredited school she owns also collects tuition fees. Which sales are VAT-exempt?

alac.answer: The fresh mangoes and the tuition fees are VAT-exempt, but the dried mangoes may be subject to VAT unless their processing is only simple.
alac.basis: Section 109(1) of the NIRC, as amended, exempts from VAT the sale or importation of agricultural and marine food products in their original state, which includes those that have undergone only simple processes of preparation or preservation for the market, and educational services rendered by private educational institutions duly accredited by the proper agency. Products that have undergone more than simple processing are not in their original state.
alac.application: Here, fresh unpeeled mangoes are agricultural food products in their original state. Dried mangoes in sealed packaging have undergone drying and packaging, which, depending on the process, may go beyond simple preservation for the market. The school is accredited and collects tuition for educational services.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the fresh mangoes and the tuition are exempt, while the dried mangoes are subject to VAT unless the drying is a simple process of preservation recognized by the rules.

keyPoints: Agricultural food products in their original state are exempt (Sec. 109)
Simple processes of preparation or preservation
Educational services of accredited private schools exempt
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 109, as amended

q: Under Section 110 of the NIRC, input tax may be credited against output tax if it is:
choices: Evidenced by a VAT invoice issued in accordance with the law, on purchases for business such as goods for sale
hints: Output tax is the VAT on sales; input tax is the VAT on purchases.
The VAT payable is output tax minus input tax.
why: NIRC Sec. 110: input tax evidenced by a VAT invoice on purchases of goods for sale, for conversion into finished products, for supplies, or for use in business, is creditable against output tax; VAT payable is output tax less allowable input tax, and any excess input tax may be carried over.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 110

q: In a quarter, a VAT-registered bakery had sales of P1 million (output VAT P120,000). It bought flour for P500,000 (input VAT P60,000, supported by VAT invoices) and a family car for the owner's personal use (VAT P90,000). It also bought sugar for P100,000 from a supplier who issued no VAT invoice. How much VAT does the bakery owe?

alac.answer: The bakery owes P60,000 in VAT.
alac.basis: Section 110(A) of the NIRC provides that input tax evidenced by a VAT invoice issued in accordance with Section 113 on purchases of goods for sale, for conversion into a finished product for sale, or for use in the course of business, shall be creditable against the output tax. VAT payable is the excess of output tax over creditable input tax. Input tax on personal purchases, or not supported by a valid VAT invoice, is not creditable.
alac.application: Here, the output VAT is P120,000. The P60,000 input VAT on flour, which is converted into bread for sale and supported by VAT invoices, is creditable. The VAT on the family car is for personal use, not business, so it is not creditable. The sugar purchase has no VAT invoice, so no input VAT can be claimed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the VAT payable is P120,000 less P60,000, or P60,000.

keyPoints: Creditable input tax: business purchases supported by VAT invoices (Sec. 110(A))
No credit for personal purchases or without VAT invoices
VAT payable = output tax less input tax
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 110

q: Under Section 112(C) of the NIRC, as amended by the Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976), the Commissioner shall decide a claim for refund of creditable input taxes within:
