choices: 90 days from the date of submission of the invoices and other supporting documents
hints: The taxpayer files the administrative claim within two years after the close of the quarter of the sale.
The taxpayer may appeal to the CTA within 30 days.
why: NIRC Sec. 112, as amended by RA 10963 and RA 11976: a VAT-registered person with zero-rated or effectively zero-rated sales may apply for refund of attributable input VAT within two years; the CIR shall decide within 90 days from submission of complete documents; the taxpayer may appeal to the CTA within 30 days from receipt of the denial or from the lapse of the 90-day period. The periods are mandatory and jurisdictional (CIR v. San Roque Power Corporation, G.R. No. 187485, February 12, 2013).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 112, as amended by RA 11976; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. San Roque Power Corporation, G.R. No. 187485, February 12, 2013

q: An exporter filed an administrative claim for refund of input VAT on its zero-rated sales, with complete documents. Without waiting for the CIR's decision, it filed a petition for review with the CTA 20 days later. Is the judicial claim proper?

alac.answer: No, the judicial claim was filed prematurely and should be dismissed.
alac.basis: Section 112 of the NIRC, as amended, gives the Commissioner ninety days from the submission of complete documents to decide a claim for refund of creditable input taxes, and allows the taxpayer to appeal to the CTA within thirty days from receipt of the decision denying the claim or after the expiration of the ninety-day period without action. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. San Roque Power Corporation, G.R. No. 187485, February 12, 2013, the Supreme Court held that the waiting period and the period to appeal are mandatory and jurisdictional, so a judicial claim filed before the CIR acts or before the period lapses is premature.
alac.application: Here, the exporter went to the CTA only 20 days after filing its administrative claim, without a decision of the CIR and before the ninety-day period expired. The CTA has no jurisdiction over a premature claim.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the petition should be dismissed; the exporter should await the CIR's decision or the lapse of the ninety days, and then appeal within thirty days.

keyPoints: CIR decides within 90 days from submission of complete documents (Sec. 112, as amended by RA 11976)
Appeal to the CTA within 30 days after denial or inaction
Periods are mandatory and jurisdictional (CIR v. San Roque)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 112, as amended by RA 11976; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. San Roque Power Corporation, G.R. No. 187485, February 12, 2013

q: Under RA 12023, which of the following is a digital service subject to VAT?
choices: Sale of rice in a market
Cloud services, online marketplaces, online search engines, online media and advertising, online platforms and digital goods
hints: RA 12023 amended Sec. 108.
Nonresident digital service providers are also covered.
why: RA 12023 amended the NIRC to impose 12% VAT on digital services consumed in the Philippines, including online search engines, e-marketplaces, cloud services, online media and advertising, online platforms and digital goods, whether supplied by resident or nonresident digital service providers.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 105 and 108, as amended by RA 12023

q: StreamCo, a foreign company with no office or employees in the Philippines, sells movie streaming subscriptions to Filipino consumers through its app. It argues that it is not subject to Philippine VAT because it has no physical presence in the country. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, StreamCo is subject to VAT as a nonresident digital service provider.
alac.basis: Section 108 of the NIRC, as amended by RA 12023, imposes a value-added tax of twelve percent on the gross sales derived from the sale or exchange of services, including digital services. RA 12023 defines digital services to include online platforms and digital goods, and a nonresident digital service provider as a digital service provider that has no physical presence in the Philippines. It subjects digital services consumed in the Philippines to VAT whether supplied by resident or nonresident providers.
alac.application: Here, StreamCo provides digital services, streaming of movies, to consumers in the Philippines. Its lack of physical presence makes it a nonresident digital service provider, which the law expressly covers.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, StreamCo is subject to 12% VAT on its subscriptions sold to Filipino consumers and must register and remit the VAT as the law requires.

keyPoints: VAT on digital services (Sec. 108, as amended by RA 12023)
Nonresident digital service provider: no physical presence
Services consumed in the Philippines are taxed
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 108, as amended by RA 12023

q: Under Section 84 of the NIRC, as amended by the TRAIN law, the estate tax rate is:
choices: Six percent (6%) of the net estate
Twelve percent (12%) of the gross estate
hints: The TRAIN law simplified the rate.
There is a standard deduction of P5 million for citizens and residents.
why: NIRC Sec. 84, as amended by RA 10963: estate tax is 6% of the net estate; Sec. 85: the gross estate of a citizen or resident includes all property wherever situated; Sec. 86: deductions include a P5 million standard deduction and the family home up to P10 million.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 84-86, as amended by RA 10963

q: Fidel, a resident citizen, died in 2025 leaving a house in Manila worth P8 million (the family home), a condominium in Tokyo worth P10 million, and bank deposits of P4 million. He had no debts. Which properties are included in his gross estate, and what is the estate tax rate?

alac.answer: All three properties are included in his gross estate, and the tax is 6% of the net estate.
alac.basis: Section 85 of the NIRC provides that the gross estate of a decedent shall include the value at the time of his death of all property, real or personal, tangible or intangible, wherever situated, except that for nonresident aliens only property situated in the Philippines is included. Section 84, as amended by RA 10963, imposes a tax at the rate of six percent based on the value of the net estate. Section 86, as amended, allows the deduction of a P5 million standard deduction and the family home up to P10 million, among others.
alac.application: Here, Fidel was a resident citizen, so his gross estate includes the Manila house, the Tokyo condominium and his deposits, totaling P22 million. From this, his estate may deduct the P5 million standard deduction and the P8 million family home, leaving a net estate of P9 million.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the estate tax is 6% of P9 million, or P540,000, subject to any other allowable deductions.

keyPoints: Gross estate of a citizen includes property wherever situated (Sec. 85)
Estate tax at 6% of net estate (Sec. 84, as amended by TRAIN)
Standard deduction and family home (Sec. 86)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 84-86, as amended by RA 10963

q: Under Section 99 of the NIRC, as amended by the TRAIN law, the donor's tax is:
choices: Six percent (6%) of total gifts in excess of P250,000 exempt gift made during the calendar year
hints: The TRAIN law removed the distinction between relatives and strangers.
The exemption is per calendar year.
why: NIRC Sec. 98: donor's tax applies to the transfer of property by gift, whether in trust or otherwise, direct or indirect; Sec. 99, as amended by RA 10963: 6% on total gifts in excess of P250,000 during the calendar year; Sec. 100: transfers for less than adequate consideration are deemed gifts to the extent of the excess (except real property under Sec. 24(D)).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 98-100, as amended by RA 10963

q: In 2025, Gina gave her son P1 million in cash in January and her friend P250,000 in June. She also sold shares of stock (not traded in the stock exchange) worth P2 million to her nephew for P1.5 million. How much is subject to donor's tax?

alac.answer: P1.5 million is subject to donor's tax, at 6%, for a tax of P90,000.
alac.basis: Section 98 of the NIRC imposes a donor's tax on the transfer of property by gift, whether direct or indirect. Section 99, as amended by RA 10963, provides that the tax for each calendar year shall be six percent computed on the basis of the total gifts in excess of the P250,000 exempt gift made during the calendar year. Section 100 provides that where property, other than real property referred to in Section 24(D), is transferred for less than an adequate and full consideration, the amount by which the fair market value exceeds the consideration shall be deemed a gift.
alac.application: Here, Gina's gifts in 2025 total P1 million to her son, P250,000 to her friend, and P500,000 deemed gift from the sale of shares to her nephew (P2 million value less P1.5 million price), or P1.75 million. Less the P250,000 annual exemption, P1.5 million is taxable.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the donor's tax is 6% of P1.5 million, or P90,000.

keyPoints: Donor's tax on direct and indirect gifts (Sec. 98)
6% on total gifts in excess of P250,000 per calendar year (Sec. 99)
Sale for less than adequate consideration is a deemed gift (Sec. 100)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 98-100, as amended by RA 10963

q: Under Section 130 of the Local Government Code, which is a fundamental principle governing local taxation?
choices: Local taxes may be confiscatory if needed
Local taxes may be collected by private persons for a fee
Taxation shall be uniform in each local government unit
hints: Section 130 lists the principles.
Collection may never be let to private persons.
why: LGC Sec. 130: local taxation shall be uniform in each LGU; taxes shall be equitable, for public purposes, not unjust, excessive, oppressive or confiscatory, and not contrary to law or in restraint of trade; collection shall not be let to private persons; revenue shall inure solely to the LGU.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 130

q: A municipality, short on staff, contracted a private company to collect its business taxes in exchange for 20% of collections. A taxpayer refused to pay the company. Is the arrangement valid?

alac.answer: No, the arrangement is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 130(c) of the Local Government Code provides, as a fundamental principle of local taxation, that the collection of local taxes, fees, charges and other impositions shall in no case be let to any private person. Section 130(b) also requires that local taxes be levied and collected only for public purposes.
alac.application: Here, the municipality let the collection of its business taxes to a private company, which would keep 20% of the collections. This is exactly what the law prohibits.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the contract is void, and the taxpayer may refuse to pay the private company, although he must still pay his taxes to the municipal treasurer.

keyPoints: Fundamental principles of local taxation (Sec. 130)
Collection may not be let to private persons
Taxes still payable to the treasurer
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 130

q: Under Section 133 of the Local Government Code, LGUs generally may NOT levy:
choices: Income tax, except when levied on banks and other financial institutions
hints: Section 133 lists common limitations.
LGUs' taxing power comes from the Constitution (Art. X, Sec. 5), subject to Congress's guidelines.
why: Art. X, Sec. 5 of the Constitution gives LGUs the power to create sources of revenue and levy taxes subject to guidelines set by Congress; LGC Sec. 129 implements it, and Sec. 133 lists common limitations, such as income tax (except on banks and financial institutions), documentary stamp tax, estate and donor's taxes, and customs duties. Sec. 186 allows taxes on other bases not taxed by the NIRC.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. X, Sec. 5; Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 129, 133 and 186

q: A city passed an ordinance imposing (a) a 1% tax on the income of all residents, and (b) a tax on billboards, a subject not taxed by the NIRC or listed in the Local Government Code, after a public hearing. Are the taxes valid?

alac.answer: The income tax is invalid, but the billboard tax may be valid.
alac.basis: Article X, Section 5 of the Constitution grants LGUs the power to create their own sources of revenue and to levy taxes, subject to guidelines and limitations provided by Congress. Section 133(a) of the Local Government Code provides that the taxing powers of LGUs shall not extend to income tax, except when levied on banks and other financial institutions. Section 186 allows LGUs to levy taxes on any base or subject not otherwise specifically enumerated in the Code or taxed under the NIRC, provided they are not unjust, excessive, oppressive or confiscatory, and the ordinance is enacted after a prior public hearing.
alac.application: Here, the 1% tax on residents' income is an income tax not levied on banks or financial institutions, which Section 133(a) prohibits. The billboard tax is on a subject neither enumerated in the Code nor taxed by the NIRC, and the ordinance was enacted after a public hearing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the income tax is void, while the billboard tax is valid if it is reasonable and complies with the other requirements.

keyPoints: Constitutional grant of taxing power (Art. X, Sec. 5)
Common limitations: no income tax except on banks (Sec. 133(a))
Residual taxing power with public hearing (Sec. 186)
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. X, Sec. 5; Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 133 and 186

q: Under Section 187 of the Local Government Code, a question on the constitutionality or legality of a tax ordinance may be raised on appeal to the Secretary of Justice within:
choices: Thirty days from the effectivity of the ordinance
hints: Public hearings are mandatory before enactment.
The appeal does not suspend the ordinance's effectivity.
why: LGC Sec. 187: public hearings are required before enacting tax ordinances; questions on their constitutionality or legality may be appealed to the Secretary of Justice within 30 days from effectivity, who decides within 60 days; the appeal does not suspend the ordinance. Failure to appeal on time is fatal (Hagonoy Market Vendor Association v. Municipality of Hagonoy, G.R. No. 137621, February 6, 2002).
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 187; Hagonoy Market Vendor Association v. Municipality of Hagonoy, G.R. No. 137621, February 6, 2002

q: A municipality enacted an ordinance raising market stall fees, effective January 1. In May, a vendors' association appealed to the Secretary of Justice, claiming that no public hearing was held. Will the appeal prosper?

alac.answer: No, the appeal will not prosper because it was filed out of time.
alac.basis: Section 187 of the Local Government Code requires public hearings before the enactment of tax ordinances and provides that any question on the constitutionality or legality of tax ordinances may be raised on appeal within thirty days from the effectivity thereof to the Secretary of Justice. In Hagonoy Market Vendor Association v. Municipality of Hagonoy, G.R. No. 137621, February 6, 2002, the Supreme Court held that the thirty-day period is mandatory, and an appeal filed beyond it, even one claiming lack of public hearing, must be dismissed.
alac.application: Here, the ordinance took effect on January 1, but the association appealed only in May, far beyond thirty days. Even if no public hearing was held, the association lost its remedy by failing to appeal on time.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Secretary of Justice should dismiss the appeal.

keyPoints: Public hearings required (Sec. 187)
Appeal to the Secretary of Justice within 30 days from effectivity
Period is mandatory (Hagonoy Market Vendor Association v. Municipality of Hagonoy)
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 187; Hagonoy Market Vendor Association v. Municipality of Hagonoy, G.R. No. 137621, February 6, 2002

q: Under Section 174 of the Local Government Code, the civil remedies of LGUs for the collection of local taxes are:
choices: Administrative action through distraint of personal property and levy upon real property, and judicial action, which may be pursued concurrently
hints: LGUs have both administrative and judicial remedies.
They may be used simultaneously.
why: LGC Sec. 174: civil remedies for collecting local taxes are (a) administrative action through distraint of personal property and levy upon real property, and (b) judicial action; either or all may be pursued concurrently at the LGU's discretion.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 174

q: A delinquent taxpayer owes a city P2 million in business taxes. The city filed a collection case in court and, at the same time, distrained the taxpayer's delivery vans. The taxpayer argues that the city must choose one remedy. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, the city may pursue both remedies at the same time.
alac.basis: Section 174 of the Local Government Code provides that the civil remedies for the collection of local taxes are (a) administrative action through distraint of goods, chattels, or other personal property, and levy upon real property, and (b) judicial action, and that either of these remedies or all may be pursued concurrently or simultaneously at the discretion of the local government unit concerned.
alac.application: Here, the city filed a judicial collection case and distrained the taxpayer's vans, which are personal property. The law expressly allows the city to use these remedies concurrently.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the taxpayer's argument fails, and the city may continue with both remedies, subject to the rule against double recovery.

keyPoints: Administrative remedies: distraint and levy (Sec. 174(a))
Judicial action (Sec. 174(b))
Remedies may be pursued concurrently
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 174

q: Under Section 194 of the Local Government Code, local taxes shall be assessed within:
choices: Two years from the date they became due
Five years from the date they became due, or ten years from discovery in case of fraud
hints: The period is longer than the NIRC's three years.
Fraud extends the period.
why: LGC Sec. 194: local taxes shall be assessed within five years from the date they became due, and collected within five years from assessment; in case of fraud or intent to evade, assessment may be made within ten years from discovery.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 194

q: In 2025, a city assessed a company for deficiency business taxes that became due in 2018. The company showed that it had filed all its returns honestly. The city argues that it has ten years to assess. Is the assessment timely?

alac.answer: No, the assessment has prescribed.
alac.basis: Section 194(a) of the Local Government Code provides that local taxes, fees, or charges shall be assessed within five years from the date they became due. Section 194(b) allows assessment within ten years from discovery only in case of fraud or intent to evade the payment of taxes.
alac.application: Here, the business taxes became due in 2018, so the city had until 2023 to assess them. The assessment in 2025 is beyond five years. The ten-year period does not apply, since the company filed honest returns and there is no fraud.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the city's right to assess has prescribed, and the assessment should be cancelled.

keyPoints: Five years from due date to assess local taxes (Sec. 194(a))
Ten years from discovery only in fraud cases (Sec. 194(b))
Prescription bars the assessment
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 194

q: May a court issue an injunction against the collection of local taxes?
choices: Never, because Sec. 218 of the NIRC applies
The Local Government Code has no provision prohibiting it, so courts may issue one, but only with great caution in view of the lifeblood doctrine
Only the Secretary of Justice may
hints: NIRC Sec. 218 covers national internal revenue taxes.
The lifeblood doctrine still applies to local taxes.
why: NIRC Sec. 218 bars injunctions only against national internal revenue taxes. The LGC contains no similar prohibition, so courts may enjoin the collection of local taxes, but must observe the requisites for injunction and the lifeblood doctrine (Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation, G.R. No. 166134, June 29, 2010).
cite: Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation, G.R. No. 166134, June 29, 2010

q: A city levied on the properties of an electric company for unpaid local franchise taxes and scheduled an auction. The company asked the RTC for an injunction, arguing that the taxes are being contested. The city argues that courts can never enjoin tax collection. Rule on the city's argument.

alac.answer: The city's argument is incorrect, but the court should grant the injunction only if the strict requisites are met, considering the lifeblood doctrine.
alac.basis: Section 218 of the NIRC prohibits courts from enjoining the collection of national internal revenue taxes, but it does not apply to local taxes. In Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation, G.R. No. 166134, June 29, 2010, the Supreme Court held that the Local Government Code does not expressly prohibit courts from issuing injunctions against the collection of local taxes, but stressed that, because taxes are the lifeblood of the government, injunctions should be issued with extreme caution and only upon a clear showing of a right in esse and of irreparable injury.
alac.application: Here, the taxes are local franchise taxes, so Section 218 does not bar an injunction. But the mere fact that the company contests the taxes is not enough; it must show a clear and unmistakable right and irreparable injury.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court may issue an injunction against the auction only if the company meets these strict requisites.

keyPoints: NIRC Sec. 218 applies only to national taxes
No express prohibition in the LGC (Angeles City v. Angeles Electric)
Lifeblood doctrine: injunction with extreme caution
cite: Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation, G.R. No. 166134, June 29, 2010

q: Under Section 195 of the Local Government Code, a taxpayer who receives a notice of assessment of local taxes may file a written protest with the local treasurer within:
choices: 60 days from receipt of the notice
hints: Otherwise, the assessment becomes final and executory.
The treasurer decides within 60 days.
why: LGC Sec. 195: protest within 60 days from receipt of the notice of assessment, or the assessment becomes final; the treasurer decides within 60 days; the taxpayer may appeal to the court within 30 days from receipt of the denial or lapse of the 60 days, or the assessment becomes conclusive.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 195

q: A store received a notice of assessment of deficiency business taxes on March 1. It filed a written protest with the city treasurer on June 15. The treasurer refused to act on the protest. What is the status of the assessment?

alac.answer: The assessment has become final and executory.
alac.basis: Section 195 of the Local Government Code provides that within sixty days from the receipt of the notice of assessment, the taxpayer may file a written protest with the local treasurer contesting the assessment; otherwise, the assessment shall become final and executory.
alac.application: Here, the store received the notice on March 1, so it had until about April 30 to protest. Its protest filed on June 15 was late. The treasurer may therefore disregard it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the assessment is final and executory, and the city may proceed to collect.

keyPoints: Protest within 60 days from receipt of the notice (Sec. 195)
Late protest: assessment becomes final and executory
City may collect
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 195

q: Under Section 196 of the Local Government Code, a court action for refund of local taxes erroneously or illegally collected must be filed:
choices: After filing a written claim for refund with the local treasurer, and within two years from the date of payment or from the date the taxpayer is entitled to a refund
Only with the Secretary of Justice
hints: A written administrative claim is a condition.
The two-year period applies to the court case.
why: LGC Sec. 196: no court case for recovery of a local tax may be maintained until a written claim for refund or credit is filed with the local treasurer, and no case shall be entertained after two years from payment or from the date the taxpayer became entitled to the refund.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 196

q: On February 1, 2023, a company paid P500,000 in local business taxes on a line of business later found not taxable. It filed a written claim for refund with the treasurer in January 2025, but the treasurer did not act. The company filed a refund case in court on March 1, 2025. Will the case prosper?

alac.answer: No, the court case is barred because it was filed beyond two years from payment.
alac.basis: Section 196 of the Local Government Code provides that no case or proceeding shall be maintained in any court for the recovery of any tax erroneously or illegally collected until a written claim for refund or credit has been filed with the local treasurer, and that no case or proceeding shall be entertained in any court after the expiration of two years from the date of the payment of such tax.
alac.application: Here, the company filed a written claim with the treasurer, satisfying the first requirement. But it paid on February 1, 2023, so it had until February 1, 2025 to file the court case. Its case filed on March 1, 2025 is late, even though its administrative claim was timely.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should dismiss the case for prescription.

keyPoints: Written claim with the treasurer required first (Sec. 196)
Court case within two years from payment
Both requirements must be met
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 196

q: If the local treasurer denies a protest against a local tax assessment, the taxpayer may appeal to the court of competent jurisdiction within:
choices: 30 days from receipt of the denial or from the lapse of the 60-day period for the treasurer to decide
hints: Otherwise the assessment becomes conclusive and unappealable.
The RTC decides; its decision may be appealed to the CTA.
why: LGC Sec. 195: the taxpayer has 30 days from receipt of the denial of the protest, or from the lapse of the 60-day period without decision, to appeal to the court of competent jurisdiction (the RTC), whose decision is appealable to the CTA; otherwise the assessment becomes conclusive and unappealable.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 195

q: A taxpayer protested a local business tax assessment on time. The treasurer did not decide the protest within 60 days. Four months after the 60 days lapsed, the treasurer finally denied the protest, and the taxpayer filed an appeal in the RTC within 30 days of the denial. Was the appeal timely?

alac.answer: No, the appeal was late; the taxpayer should have appealed within 30 days from the lapse of the 60-day period.
alac.basis: Section 195 of the Local Government Code provides that the local treasurer shall decide the protest within sixty days from its filing, and that the taxpayer shall have thirty days from the receipt of the denial of the protest or from the lapse of the sixty-day period within which to appeal with the court of competent jurisdiction; otherwise, the assessment becomes conclusive and unappealable.
alac.application: Here, the treasurer's inaction for sixty days triggered the taxpayer's thirty-day period to appeal. The taxpayer waited for the treasurer's late denial instead and appealed about five months after the sixty days lapsed. The later denial did not revive the lapsed period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the appeal was filed out of time, and the assessment has become conclusive and unappealable.

keyPoints: Treasurer decides within 60 days (Sec. 195)
Appeal within 30 days from denial or from lapse of the 60 days
Late appeal: assessment conclusive and unappealable
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 195

q: Under Section 198 of the Local Government Code, real property shall be classified for assessment purposes on the basis of:
hints: Use, not ownership, determines classification.
Appraisal is at current and fair market value.
why: LGC Sec. 198: real property is appraised at its current and fair market value, classified on the basis of its actual use, assessed on a uniform classification within each LGU, and the appraisal and collection may not be let to private persons.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 198

q: A lot titled and declared as "residential" is actually used as a gasoline station. The assessor reclassified it as commercial and applied the higher commercial assessment level. The owner objects, citing the title. Is the reclassification proper?

alac.answer: Yes, the reclassification is proper.
alac.basis: Section 198 of the Local Government Code provides that real property shall be appraised at its current and fair market value, and shall be classified for assessment purposes on the basis of its actual use. Section 199(b) defines actual use as the purpose for which the property is principally or predominantly utilized by the person in possession thereof.
alac.application: Here, although the title and tax declaration state "residential," the lot is actually and principally used as a gasoline station, a commercial use. Classification follows actual use, not the description in the title.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the assessor properly reclassified the lot as commercial.

keyPoints: Classification based on actual use (Sec. 198(b))
Actual use defined (Sec. 199(b))
Title description not controlling
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 198 and 199

q: Under Section 234 of the Local Government Code, real property owned by the Republic of the Philippines is exempt from real property tax, except when:
choices: Its beneficial use has been granted, for consideration or otherwise, to a taxable person
hints: The exemption follows beneficial use.
Charitable property is exempt only if actually, directly and exclusively used for charitable purposes.
why: LGC Sec. 234: exempt are (a) government property, except when beneficial use is granted to a taxable person; (b) property actually, directly and exclusively used for religious, charitable or educational purposes; (c) certain machinery of water and power utilities and GOCCs; (d) property of registered cooperatives; and (e) certain pollution control equipment. Portions of a charitable hospital leased to private businesses are taxable (Lung Center of the Philippines v. Quezon City, G.R. No. 144104, June 29, 2004).
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 234; Lung Center of the Philippines v. Quezon City, G.R. No. 144104, June 29, 2004

q: A charitable hospital leases portions of its building to private clinics and a pharmacy, and uses the rest to treat patients, including charity patients. The city assessed real property tax on the whole building. Is the hospital exempt?

alac.answer: The hospital is exempt only as to the portions actually, directly and exclusively used for its charitable purposes; the leased portions are taxable.
alac.basis: Section 234(b) of the Local Government Code exempts from real property tax charitable institutions and all lands, buildings, and improvements actually, directly, and exclusively used for charitable purposes. In Lung Center of the Philippines v. Quezon City, G.R. No. 144104, June 29, 2004, the Supreme Court held that a charitable hospital is exempt only as to the portions of its property actually, directly and exclusively used for charitable purposes, and that the portions leased to private entities are subject to real property tax.
alac.application: Here, the portions used to treat patients are used for the hospital's charitable purpose. The portions leased to private clinics and a pharmacy are used for commercial purposes and earn rent, so they are not exclusively used for charity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the city may tax only the leased portions, and the rest of the building is exempt.

keyPoints: Exemption of property actually, directly and exclusively used for charity (Sec. 234(b))
Partial exemption (Lung Center v. Quezon City)
Leased portions taxable
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 234; Lung Center of the Philippines v. Quezon City, G.R. No. 144104, June 29, 2004

q: Under the Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RA 12001), the schedule of market values (SMV) of an LGU is prepared by:
choices: The provincial, city and municipal assessors, following the Philippine Valuation Standards and DOF rules
hints: The Secretary of Finance certifies compliance with the valuation standards.
SMVs are updated every three years.
why: RA 12001 Sec. 15: assessors prepare the SMV under the Philippine Valuation Standards; Sec. 16: the Secretary of Finance certifies its compliance; Sec. 19: SMVs are updated every three years. LGC Sec. 201: all real property, taxable or exempt, is appraised at current and fair market value.
cite: Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RA 12001), Secs. 15, 16 and 19; Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 201

q: A city's assessor last revised its schedule of market values in 2010. After RA 12001 took effect, a property owner asked whether the city may keep using the 2010 values indefinitely, and whether the BIR zonal values automatically replace them. Advise the owner.

alac.answer: No, the city must update its schedule of market values as RA 12001 requires; BIR zonal values do not automatically replace it.
alac.basis: Section 201 of the Local Government Code requires all real property to be appraised at the current and fair market value prevailing in the locality. RA 12001 provides that the assessors shall prepare the SMVs pursuant to the Philippine Valuation Standards (Section 15), that the Secretary of Finance certifies their compliance (Section 16), and that assessors shall update their SMVs within two years from the effectivity of the Act and every three years thereafter (Section 19).
alac.application: Here, the 2010 SMV is outdated and no longer reflects current and fair market values. Under RA 12001, the city must update it within two years from the law's effectivity and every three years after that, through its assessors, subject to the Secretary of Finance's certification.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the city may not keep using its 2010 values indefinitely and must update its SMV under RA 12001.

keyPoints: Appraisal at current and fair market value (LGC Sec. 201)
Preparation of SMVs by assessors under the PVS (RA 12001, Sec. 15)
Updating within two years, then every three years (Sec. 19)
cite: Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RA 12001), Secs. 15, 16 and 19; Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 201

q: Under Section 270 of the Local Government Code, the basic real property tax shall be collected within:
choices: One year from the date it became due
Five years from the date it became due, or ten years from discovery in case of fraud
hints: Remedies: levy on real property or judicial action (Sec. 256).
Interest is 2% per month, up to 36 months (Sec. 255).
why: LGC Sec. 270: RPT shall be collected within five years from the date it became due, or within ten years from discovery of fraud; Sec. 256: the LGU may collect by administrative levy on real property or by judicial action; Sec. 255: unpaid RPT earns 2% interest per month, up to 36 months.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 255, 256 and 270

q: A lot owner has not paid real property tax for six years, from 2019 to 2024. In 2025, the city treasurer issued a warrant of levy for all six years, plus interest at 2% a month for the full period. What may the city validly collect?

alac.answer: The city may collect only the taxes that have not prescribed, with interest capped at 36 months per unpaid tax.
alac.basis: Section 270 of the Local Government Code provides that the basic real property tax shall be collected within five years from the date it becomes due, except in case of fraud. Section 256 allows the LGU to collect by administrative levy on real property or by judicial action. Section 255 imposes interest at two percent per month on unpaid real property tax, provided that in no case shall the total interest exceed thirty-six months.
alac.application: Here, the tax for 2019 became due in 2019; by 2025, more than five years had passed, so its collection has prescribed absent fraud, while the taxes for 2020 to 2024 may still be collected by levy. The interest on each year's unpaid tax cannot exceed thirty-six months.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the levy is valid for the 2020 to 2024 taxes, with interest not exceeding 36 months each, but not for the prescribed 2019 tax.

keyPoints: Five-year period to collect RPT (Sec. 270)
Administrative levy or judicial action (Sec. 256)
Interest at 2% per month, maximum 36 months (Sec. 255)
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 255, 256 and 270

q: Under Section 252 of the Local Government Code, a protest against a real property tax assessment will be entertained only if:
choices: The taxpayer first pays the tax, with "paid under protest" annotated on the receipt
hints: Pay first, then protest.
Exception: when the assessor's authority or the legality of the tax itself is questioned.
why: LGC Sec. 252: no protest shall be entertained unless the taxpayer first pays the tax; the protest must be filed within 30 days from payment and decided within 60 days. Payment under protest is not required when the taxpayer questions the authority to assess or the legality of the tax itself, as distinguished from the reasonableness of the assessment (Ty v. Trampe, G.R. No. 117577, December 1, 1995).
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 252; Ty v. Trampe, G.R. No. 117577, December 1, 1995

q: Owners of properties in a municipality questioned new real property tax assessments, arguing that the schedule of market values was void because it was prepared by the municipal assessor alone, contrary to the law requiring a joint schedule. They went to court without paying the taxes under protest. Must they first pay under protest?

alac.answer: No, they need not first pay under protest, because they question the legality and authority behind the assessment, not its reasonableness.
alac.basis: Section 252 of the Local Government Code provides that no protest shall be entertained unless the taxpayer first pays the tax. However, in Ty v. Trampe, G.R. No. 117577, December 1, 1995, the Supreme Court held that payment under protest is not required when the taxpayer does not question the reasonableness of the amount assessed but the very authority and power of the assessor to impose the assessment, or the validity of the schedule on which it is based, since that is a purely legal question.
alac.application: Here, the owners do not claim that the assessed values are excessive; they claim that the schedule of market values itself is void because it was prepared without legal authority. That is a question of law on the authority of the assessor.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the owners may go directly to court without first paying the taxes under protest.

keyPoints: Payment under protest generally required (Sec. 252)
Exception: questions of authority or legality, not reasonableness (Ty v. Trampe)
Direct resort to court allowed
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 252; Ty v. Trampe, G.R. No. 117577, December 1, 1995

q: Under Section 276 of the Local Government Code, the sanggunian may condone or reduce real property taxes and interest in case of:
choices: General failure of crops, substantial decrease in the price of agricultural products, or calamity
A request from a rich taxpayer
hints: Relief must be granted by ordinance.
RA 12001 also granted a one-time amnesty on RPT penalties.
why: LGC Sec. 276: the sanggunian, by ordinance passed before January 1 and upon recommendation of the disaster council, may condone or reduce RPT and interest for succeeding years in case of crop failure, price decrease of agricultural products or calamity. RA 12001 Sec. 30 granted an amnesty on penalties, surcharges and interest on unpaid RPT, availed within two years.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 276; Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RA 12001), Sec. 30

q: After a strong typhoon devastated farms in a municipality, the mayor, by executive order issued in March, reduced by half the real property taxes for that same year. A councilor questions the order. Separately, a delinquent owner asks whether he can avoid the penalties on his unpaid RPT for past years. Advise them.

alac.answer: The mayor's order is invalid; condonation must be made by the sanggunian through an ordinance passed before January 1 for succeeding years. The delinquent owner may avail of the RA 12001 amnesty on penalties within its period.
alac.basis: Section 276 of the Local Government Code provides that in case of a general failure of crops, a substantial decrease in the price of agricultural products, or calamity, the sanggunian concerned, by ordinance passed prior to the first day of January of any year and upon recommendation of the disaster coordinating council, may condone or reduce, wholly or partially, the taxes and interest thereon for the succeeding year or years. Section 30 of RA 12001 grants a real property tax amnesty covering penalties, surcharges and interest on unpaid real property taxes prior to its effectivity, which may be availed within two years after its effectivity.
alac.application: Here, the reduction was made by the mayor, not the sanggunian, by executive order, not ordinance, in March, and for the current year, not succeeding years. It does not comply with Section 276. The delinquent owner, on the other hand, may pay his basic tax and have penalties, surcharges and interest waived under the RA 12001 amnesty if he avails within the two-year window.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the mayor's order is void, and the owner may use the RA 12001 amnesty to settle his past RPT without penalties.

keyPoints: Condonation by sanggunian ordinance before January 1, for succeeding years (Sec. 276)
Grounds: crop failure, price decrease, calamity
RA 12001 amnesty on RPT penalties within two years
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 276; Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RA 12001), Sec. 30

q: Under Section 226 of the Local Government Code, a property owner dissatisfied with the assessor's assessment may appeal to the Local Board of Assessment Appeals (LBAA) within:
choices: 60 days from receipt of the written notice of assessment
hints: The LBAA decides within 120 days (Sec. 229).
The appeal is by petition under oath.
why: LGC Sec. 226: appeal to the provincial or city LBAA within 60 days from receipt of the written notice of assessment, by petition under oath with supporting documents; Sec. 229: the LBAA decides within 120 days.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 226 and 229

q: Hilda received a notice of a new assessment of her land, which she believes is overvalued. Instead of appealing, she wrote the mayor a letter asking for reconsideration. Ninety days later, the mayor told her he has no authority. She then appealed to the LBAA. Will her appeal prosper?

alac.answer: No, her appeal is late and will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 226 of the Local Government Code provides that any owner who is not satisfied with the action of the assessor in the assessment of his property may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the written notice of assessment, appeal to the Local Board of Assessment Appeals by filing a petition under oath. The LBAA shall decide the appeal within 120 days (Section 229).
alac.application: Here, Hilda contests the valuation of her land, which is a matter for the LBAA. Her letter to the mayor, who has no authority over assessments, did not stop the running of the sixty-day period. By the time she appealed to the LBAA, more than sixty days had passed since she received the notice.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, her appeal is late, and the assessment has become final.

keyPoints: Appeal to the LBAA within 60 days from receipt of the notice (Sec. 226)
Letter to the mayor does not stop the period
LBAA decides within 120 days (Sec. 229)
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 226 and 229

q: A decision of the Local Board of Assessment Appeals may be appealed to:
choices: The Central Board of Assessment Appeals (CBAA), within 30 days from receipt of the decision
hints: The CBAA's members are appointed by the President.
CBAA decisions are appealable to the CTA en banc.
why: LGC Sec. 229(c): the owner or assessor may appeal the LBAA's decision to the CBAA within 30 days from receipt; Sec. 230: the CBAA is composed of a chairman and two members appointed by the President; its decisions are appealable to the CTA en banc (RA 9282).
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 229 and 230

q: The LBAA ruled against Ivan on the valuation of his commercial building. He wants to go directly to the Court of Tax Appeals. Advise him on the correct remedy.

alac.answer: Ivan must first appeal to the Central Board of Assessment Appeals within 30 days; only the CBAA's decision may be brought to the CTA en banc.
alac.basis: Under the Local Government Code, the decision of the Local Board of Assessment Appeals may be appealed by the owner or the assessor to the Central Board of Assessment Appeals within thirty days from receipt (Section 229(c)), and the CBAA is composed of a chairman and two members appointed by the President (Section 230). Under RA 9282, the CTA en banc has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions of the CBAA in cases involving the assessment and taxation of real property originally decided by the provincial or city board of assessment appeals.
alac.application: Here, Ivan has an adverse LBAA decision on the valuation of his building. The CTA's jurisdiction over real property assessment cases covers decisions of the CBAA, not of the LBAA.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivan should appeal to the CBAA within 30 days, and only then, if he loses, to the CTA en banc.

keyPoints: LBAA decision appealable to the CBAA within 30 days (Sec. 229(c))
CBAA composition (Sec. 230)
CTA en banc reviews CBAA decisions (RA 9282)
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 229 and 230; Court of Tax Appeals law (RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282)

q: Under Section 231 of the Local Government Code, an appeal on the assessment of real property:
choices: Suspends the collection of the tax
Shall in no case suspend the collection of the corresponding realty taxes, without prejudice to later adjustment
hints: Taxes must be paid while the appeal is pending.
The lifeblood doctrine again.
why: LGC Sec. 231: an appeal on assessments shall in no case suspend the collection of the realty taxes as assessed, without prejudice to subsequent adjustment depending on the outcome of the appeal.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 231

q: Jaime appealed his property assessment to the LBAA and stopped paying his real property tax while the appeal was pending, believing that the appeal suspends payment. The city treasurer issued a notice of delinquency. Is the treasurer correct?

alac.answer: Yes, the treasurer is correct; the appeal does not suspend the payment of the tax.
alac.basis: Section 231 of the Local Government Code provides that an appeal on assessments of real property shall, in no case, suspend the collection of the corresponding realty taxes on the property involved as assessed by the assessor, without prejudice to subsequent adjustment depending upon the final outcome of the appeal.
alac.application: Here, Jaime's appeal to the LBAA did not suspend his obligation to pay the tax as assessed. By not paying while the appeal was pending, he became delinquent, and the treasurer may impose interest and enforce collection.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the notice of delinquency is proper; if Jaime wins his appeal, the excess he pays will be refunded or credited.

keyPoints: Appeal does not suspend collection (Sec. 231)
Taxpayer must pay as assessed
Adjustment after the outcome of the appeal
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 231

q: Under Section 139 of the Local Government Code, the professional tax is levied by:
choices: The province, on persons engaged in the practice of a profession requiring government examination, not exceeding P300 a year
hints: The tax is paid where the professional practices or has a principal office.
Payment allows practice anywhere in the Philippines.
why: LGC Sec. 139: the province may levy an annual professional tax, not exceeding P300, on persons practicing a profession requiring government examination; it is paid where the professional practices or has a principal office, and entitles him to practice anywhere in the Philippines.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 139

q: Atty. Kim maintains her principal law office in Pasig but appears in courts in Cebu and Davao. Cebu City demands that she pay its professional tax before she can appear in its courts. Must she pay?

alac.answer: No, she need not pay Cebu City's professional tax if she has paid where she maintains her principal office.
alac.basis: Section 139 of the Local Government Code provides that every person legally authorized to practice his profession shall pay the professional tax to the province where he practices his profession or where he maintains his principal office in case he practices in several places, and that a person who has paid the corresponding professional tax shall be entitled to practice his profession in any part of the Philippines without being subjected to any other national or local tax, license, or fee for the practice of such profession.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Kim practices in several places, so she pays the professional tax where she maintains her principal office, Pasig (which, as a Metro Manila city, may levy the tax). Having paid it there, she may practice in Cebu and Davao without paying their professional taxes.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Cebu City cannot require her to pay its professional tax.

keyPoints: Professional tax levied by the province (or city) (Sec. 139)
Paid where the principal office is, if practicing in several places
Entitles practice anywhere in the Philippines
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 139

q: Under Section 143 of the Local Government Code, the local business tax of manufacturers is generally based on:
choices: Their gross sales or receipts for the preceding calendar year
hints: It is a tax on the privilege of doing business.
Each line of business is taxed separately.
why: LGC Sec. 143: municipalities (and cities under Sec. 151) may impose business taxes on manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, contractors, banks and other businesses, generally based on gross sales or receipts for the preceding calendar year, according to the graduated schedules.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 143 and 151

q: A company manufactures canned goods in a factory in Laguna and sells them through a branch sales office in Makati. Both the Laguna municipality and Makati City want to tax all of its gross sales. How should the business tax be allocated?

alac.answer: The sales should be allocated according to the situs rules: sales recorded in the Makati branch are taxable by Makati, and the remaining sales are divided between the factory site and the principal office under the allocation in the Code.
alac.basis: Section 143 of the Local Government Code allows municipalities, and under Section 151 cities, to impose a business tax on manufacturers based on their gross sales or receipts for the preceding calendar year. Section 150 provides that sales made through a branch or sales outlet shall be recorded in and taxable by the LGU where the branch is located, and that sales recorded in the principal office are allocated thirty percent to the LGU of the principal office and seventy percent to the LGU where the factory is located.
alac.application: Here, the canned goods are sold through the Makati branch, so those sales are recorded there and taxed by Makati. The Laguna municipality, where the factory is, may tax its share under the 30-70 allocation only of sales recorded in the principal office, not the branch sales.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, each LGU may tax only the sales allocated to it, and the company should not be taxed twice on the same sales.

keyPoints: Business tax based on gross sales of the preceding year (Sec. 143)
Branch sales taxable where the branch is (Sec. 150)
30-70 allocation between principal office and factory
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 143, 150 and 151

q: Under Section 157 of the Local Government Code, an individual liable to community tax pays a basic tax of P5 and an additional tax based on:
choices: Gross receipts or earnings from business or exercise of profession, salaries, or income from real property, up to a maximum
hints: Community tax is levied by cities and municipalities (Sec. 156).
The additional tax has a ceiling.
why: LGC Secs. 156-157: cities and municipalities may levy a community tax; individuals 18 or older who are employed, in business, own real property of P1,000 assessed value or more, or must file income tax returns pay P5 plus P1 for every P1,000 of gross receipts, earnings or real property income, up to P5,000.
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 156 and 157

q: Lino, 25, has been employed for a year and earns a salary of P600,000 a year. His city requires him to pay community tax. He argues that, since he already pays income tax, the community tax is double taxation. Must he pay, and how much is the additional tax?

alac.answer: Yes, he must pay; his additional community tax is P600, on top of the P5 basic tax.
alac.basis: Section 156 of the Local Government Code allows cities and municipalities to levy a community tax. Section 157 provides that every inhabitant of the Philippines eighteen years of age or over who has been regularly employed on a wage or salary basis for at least thirty consecutive working days during any calendar year shall pay a basic community tax of P5 and an additional tax of P1 for every P1,000 of income from salaries, among others, not exceeding P5,000. Taxes imposed by different taxing authorities for different purposes are not prohibited double taxation.
alac.application: Here, Lino is 25 and has been regularly employed for a year, so he is liable to community tax. His P600,000 salary results in an additional tax of P1 for every P1,000, or P600, below the P5,000 cap. The community tax and the national income tax are imposed by different authorities on different bases.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lino must pay P605 in community tax, and there is no prohibited double taxation.

keyPoints: Community tax levied by cities and municipalities (Sec. 156)
Basic P5 plus P1 per P1,000 of salary, up to P5,000 (Sec. 157)
Not prohibited double taxation
cite: Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Secs. 156 and 157

q: What is the difference between a tax deficiency and a tax delinquency?
choices: A deficiency is the amount by which the correct tax exceeds the tax shown in the return; a delinquency is the failure to pay a tax due on time, including an assessed deficiency not paid within the period in the notice
hints: Deficiency interest and delinquency interest are not imposed simultaneously (Sec. 249(A)).
An assessed deficiency becomes delinquent if unpaid on the due date.
why: A deficiency tax is the excess of the correct tax over the amount reported; a delinquency arises when a tax due (including an assessed deficiency) is not paid on time. Under Sec. 249, as amended by TRAIN, interest is double the legal rate, and deficiency and delinquency interest shall not be imposed simultaneously.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 249, as amended by RA 10963

q: A taxpayer's 2023 return showed an income tax due of P1 million, which he paid. A BIR audit found the correct tax to be P1.5 million, and a final assessment with a due date of payment was issued. He did not pay by the due date. What is the nature of his liability before and after the due date, and how is interest imposed?

alac.answer: The P500,000 is a deficiency tax until the due date in the assessment; after that, it becomes a delinquency, and only one kind of interest runs at a time.
alac.basis: A deficiency tax is the amount by which the correct tax exceeds the tax shown in the return. When an assessed deficiency is not paid within the time prescribed in the notice of assessment, the taxpayer becomes delinquent. Section 249 of the NIRC, as amended by RA 10963, imposes interest at double the legal interest rate on any unpaid tax and provides that in no case shall the deficiency and the delinquency interest be imposed simultaneously.
alac.application: Here, the P500,000 difference between the correct tax and the tax paid is a deficiency, which earns deficiency interest from the original due date until full payment or the issuance of the notice and demand, whichever comes first. When he failed to pay by the due date in the assessment, the deficiency became delinquent, subject to delinquency interest and the surcharge.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is liable for the deficiency tax with deficiency interest, and upon delinquency, for delinquency interest and surcharge, but not both kinds of interest for the same period.

keyPoints: Deficiency: correct tax exceeds tax reported
Delinquency: failure to pay on the due date
No simultaneous deficiency and delinquency interest (Sec. 249)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 249, as amended by RA 10963

q: Under Section 228 of the NIRC, if the taxpayer is not informed in writing of the law and the facts on which the assessment is made:
choices: The CIR may simply re-send it
hints: Due process applies to tax assessments.
The PAN must also be duly received (CIR v. Metro Star Superama).
why: NIRC Sec. 228: the taxpayer shall be informed in writing of the law and the facts on which the assessment is made; otherwise, the assessment is void. Failure to show that the taxpayer received the PAN violates due process and voids the assessment (CIR v. Metro Star Superama, Inc., G.R. No. 185371, December 8, 2010).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Metro Star Superama, Inc., G.R. No. 185371, December 8, 2010

q: The BIR issued a Final Assessment Notice to a company without first issuing a Preliminary Assessment Notice, and the company denied ever receiving any notice before the FAN. The BIR could not prove that a PAN was sent and received. No exception under Section 228 applies. Is the assessment valid?

alac.answer: No, the assessment is void for violation of due process.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC requires the Commissioner to first notify the taxpayer of his findings, except in specified cases, and to inform the taxpayer in writing of the law and the facts on which the assessment is made; otherwise, the assessment shall be void. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Metro Star Superama, Inc., G.R. No. 185371, December 8, 2010, the Supreme Court held that the sending and receipt of the PAN is part of due process, and that an assessment issued without proof that the taxpayer received the PAN is void.
alac.application: Here, no exception applies, the BIR could not prove that it sent and the company received a PAN, and the FAN was issued directly. The company was deprived of the chance to respond before the final assessment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the assessment is void, and the BIR cannot collect on it.

keyPoints: Pre-assessment notice required except in listed cases (Sec. 228)
Receipt of the PAN is part of due process (CIR v. Metro Star Superama)
Assessment violating due process is void
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Metro Star Superama, Inc., G.R. No. 185371, December 8, 2010

q: According to Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fitness by Design, Inc., a Final Assessment Notice is void if:
choices: It is signed by the CIR
It does not contain a definite demand to pay the tax within a specific period (it lacks a definite due date)
It is printed on colored paper
hints: A valid assessment must demand payment within a period.
It must also state the law and facts (Sec. 228).
why: A valid assessment must (1) be in writing, (2) state the law and facts on which it is based, (3) contain a demand for payment within a specific period, and (4) be issued by an authorized officer within the prescriptive period; an FAN without a definite due date is void (CIR v. Fitness by Design, Inc., G.R. No. 215957, November 9, 2016).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fitness by Design, Inc., G.R. No. 215957, November 9, 2016

q: A FAN computed a company's deficiency taxes with interest "until fully paid," but stated no definite due date for payment, saying only that the amounts are "subject to change." The company did not protest within 30 days, and the BIR began collection. The company argues that the FAN is void. Is it correct?

alac.answer: Yes, the company is correct; the FAN is void, so it never became final.
alac.basis: In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fitness by Design, Inc., G.R. No. 215957, November 9, 2016, the Supreme Court held that a final assessment notice that does not contain a definite demand to pay the tax within a specific period, and whose amounts are subject to change because interest is computed until fully paid without a due date, is not a valid assessment. A void assessment does not become final and executory even without a protest, and it cannot be the basis for collection.
alac.application: Here, the FAN stated no definite due date and described the amounts as subject to change. It did not make a definite demand for payment within a fixed period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the FAN is void, the failure to protest did not make it final, and the BIR cannot collect on it.

keyPoints: Requisites of a valid assessment
Definite demand to pay within a specific period (CIR v. Fitness by Design)
Void assessment does not become final
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Fitness by Design, Inc., G.R. No. 215957, November 9, 2016

q: In tax assessments, who has the burden of proof?
choices: Assessments are presumed correct, so the taxpayer has the burden to show that they are wrong; but an assessment must have a factual basis and cannot rest on mere presumptions
The BIR must always prove everything
hints: The presumption of correctness is not absolute.
Unauthenticated photocopies are not 'best evidence obtainable'.
why: Tax assessments are presumed correct and made in good faith, and the taxpayer must prove otherwise; but the presumption does not apply when the assessment is not based on facts. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Hantex Trading Co., Inc., G.R. No. 136975, March 31, 2005, an assessment based on unauthenticated photocopies was void. NIRC Sec. 6(B) allows assessment on the best evidence obtainable.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 6(B); Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Hantex Trading Co., Inc., G.R. No. 136975, March 31, 2005

q: The BIR assessed a trading company P20 million in deficiency income tax, based solely on unauthenticated photocopies of import entries obtained from an informant, as the company had no books. The company presented its own computations showing lower income. Who should prevail?

alac.answer: The company should prevail; the assessment is not supported by competent evidence.
alac.basis: Section 6(B) of the NIRC allows the Commissioner to assess the proper tax on the best evidence obtainable when a report is not forthcoming. As a rule, assessments are presumed correct, and the taxpayer has the burden to prove otherwise. But in Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Hantex Trading Co., Inc., G.R. No. 136975, March 31, 2005, the Supreme Court held that the best evidence obtainable does not include mere unauthenticated photocopies, and that an assessment based on them has no factual basis and is void, so the presumption of correctness does not arise.
alac.application: Here, the BIR relied solely on unauthenticated photocopies of import entries from an informant. That is not competent evidence, so the assessment lacks a factual foundation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the presumption of correctness does not apply, and the assessment should be cancelled.

keyPoints: Assessments presumed correct; taxpayer bears the burden
Best evidence obtainable (Sec. 6(B))
Assessment based on unauthenticated photocopies is void (CIR v. Hantex)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 6(B); Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Hantex Trading Co., Inc., G.R. No. 136975, March 31, 2005

q: Under Section 13 of the NIRC, a revenue officer may examine a taxpayer pursuant to:
choices: A Letter of Authority issued by the Revenue Regional Director (or the CIR)
A memorandum from any BIR employee
hints: An assessment without a valid LOA is void (Medicard v. CIR).
The LOA covers only the periods and officers named.
why: NIRC Sec. 13: revenue officers examine taxpayers pursuant to a Letter of Authority; an assessment made without a valid LOA is void (Medicard Philippines, Inc. v. CIR, G.R. No. 222743, April 5, 2017), and an LOA covering 'the period ... and unverified prior years' is limited to the specific period stated (CIR v. Sony Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 178697, November 17, 2010).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 13; Medicard Philippines, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 222743, April 5, 2017

q: A revenue officer audited a company based only on a Letter Notice from the BIR's computerized matching program, without any Letter of Authority, and recommended a deficiency VAT assessment, which the BIR issued. Is the assessment valid?

alac.answer: No, the assessment is void.
alac.basis: Section 13 of the NIRC provides that a revenue officer may examine taxpayers pursuant to a Letter of Authority issued by the Revenue Regional Director, and Section 6(A) gives the Commissioner or his duly authorized representative the power to examine returns and assess taxes. In Medicard Philippines, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 222743, April 5, 2017, the Supreme Court held that a Letter Notice is not a substitute for a Letter of Authority, and that an assessment issued without a valid LOA violates the taxpayer's right to due process and is void.
alac.application: Here, the revenue officer examined the company's records on the basis of a Letter Notice only, without a Letter of Authority. He had no authority to examine and recommend an assessment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the deficiency VAT assessment is void.

keyPoints: Examination requires a Letter of Authority (Sec. 13)
A Letter Notice is not a substitute (Medicard v. CIR)
Assessment without LOA is void
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 6 and 13; Medicard Philippines, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 222743, April 5, 2017

q: During a tax audit, when the revenue officer requests the taxpayer's books and records, the taxpayer:
choices: May ignore the request without consequence
Should submit them, since the CIR may otherwise assess on the best evidence obtainable, and may be penalized for refusal
Must submit only to the court
hints: The CIR may obtain information and examine books (Sec. 5).
Failure to submit allows a best-evidence assessment (Sec. 6(B)).
why: The CIR may examine books and records and obtain information from the taxpayer and others (NIRC Secs. 5 and 6); if the taxpayer does not submit records, the CIR may assess on the best evidence obtainable (Sec. 6(B)), and the taxpayer may be penalized for failure to obey a summons.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 5 and 6

q: During an audit under a valid Letter of Authority, a taxpayer refused to submit his books of accounts, saying they were "confidential." The BIR then assessed him using third-party information on his purchases and sales. Later, in his protest, he submitted the books for the first time. Is the BIR's assessment proper?

alac.answer: Yes, the BIR could assess on the best evidence obtainable, although it should consider the books he later submits with his protest.
alac.basis: Section 6(A) and (B) of the NIRC authorize the Commissioner to examine the taxpayer's books and records, and provide that when a report required by law is not forthcoming, or there is reason to believe it is false, the Commissioner shall assess the proper tax on the best evidence obtainable. Section 5 allows the Commissioner to obtain information from third parties. The taxpayer may submit relevant supporting documents within sixty days from filing his protest (Section 228).
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer refused to produce his books during the audit, so the BIR was entitled to use third-party information on his purchases and sales as the best evidence obtainable. His books, submitted with his protest, are supporting documents that the BIR must evaluate in deciding the protest.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the assessment was properly made, but the BIR should consider the books when it decides the protest.

keyPoints: Power to examine books (Sec. 6(A))
Best evidence obtainable when records are not produced (Sec. 6(B))
Supporting documents within 60 days from protest (Sec. 228)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 5, 6 and 228

q: Under the current BIR audit rules (RR 12-99, as amended by RR 22-2020), the Notice of Discrepancy (NOD):
choices: Informs the taxpayer of the audit findings and gives him the opportunity to explain them before a PAN is issued
hints: The NOD replaced the old informal conference.
If not resolved, a PAN follows.
why: Under RR 12-99, as amended by RR 22-2020, the taxpayer is informed of the discrepancies through a Notice of Discrepancy and given the chance to present his side (within 5 days, followed by a discussion of the discrepancy); if unresolved, the case proceeds to a PAN, in keeping with the due process required by NIRC Sec. 228.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Revenue Regulations No. 12-99, as amended by Revenue Regulations No. 22-2020

q: After an audit, a revenue officer found discrepancies in a company's sales. Instead of issuing a Notice of Discrepancy, the BIR immediately issued a PAN. The company argues that it was denied the chance to explain. What is the purpose of the NOD, and what is the effect of skipping it?

alac.answer: The NOD gives the taxpayer the first chance to explain the audit findings; skipping it denies part of the due process the rules require, and the resulting assessment may be challenged as void.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC requires the Commissioner to first notify the taxpayer of his findings before assessment. Revenue Regulations No. 12-99, as amended by RR 22-2020, implement this by requiring a Notice of Discrepancy, through which the taxpayer is informed of the discrepancies and given the opportunity to present his side and documents, before a PAN is issued. Because the right to be informed and heard in the assessment process is part of due process, a failure to follow the required steps may render the assessment void, as in Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Metro Star Superama, Inc., G.R. No. 185371, December 8, 2010.
alac.application: Here, the BIR went directly to the PAN without first informing the company of the discrepancies through an NOD. The company lost its first opportunity to explain the findings at the audit level.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company may challenge the assessment for denial of due process, and the BIR should have issued the NOD first.

keyPoints: NOD informs the taxpayer of discrepancies and lets him explain (RR 22-2020)
Part of the due process in Sec. 228
Failure to observe required steps may void the assessment
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Revenue Regulations No. 12-99, as amended by Revenue Regulations No. 22-2020; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Metro Star Superama, Inc., G.R. No. 185371, December 8, 2010

q: Under Section 228 of the NIRC, a Preliminary Assessment Notice is NOT required when:
choices: The finding is the result of a mathematical error in the computation of the tax appearing on the face of the return
hints: Section 228 lists five exceptions.
Another exception: excise tax due on exciseable articles not paid.
why: NIRC Sec. 228: no PAN is required when (a) the deficiency results from a mathematical error on the face of the return; (b) there is a discrepancy between tax withheld and tax remitted; (c) excess creditable withholding tax was carried over and also claimed as refund; (d) excise tax on exciseable articles was not paid; or (e) an exempt person's tax-free purchases were transferred to non-exempt persons.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: A withholding agent's records showed that it withheld P2 million in taxes from its employees, but it remitted only P1.5 million to the BIR. The BIR issued a FAN for the P500,000 difference without a PAN. The agent argues that the FAN is void for lack of a PAN. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, the agent is not correct; no PAN was required.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC requires the Commissioner to first notify the taxpayer of his findings through a pre-assessment notice, but provides that a pre-assessment notice shall not be required, among others, when a discrepancy has been determined between the tax withheld and the amount actually remitted by the withholding agent.
alac.application: Here, the BIR found a discrepancy between the P2 million withheld and the P1.5 million remitted by the withholding agent. That falls squarely within the exception.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the FAN is not void for lack of a PAN, although it must still state the law and facts on which it is based.

keyPoints: PAN generally required (Sec. 228)
Exception: discrepancy between tax withheld and remitted
FAN must still state law and facts
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: Under Section 228 of the NIRC, a taxpayer may protest a Final Assessment Notice / Formal Letter of Demand by filing a request for reconsideration or reinvestigation within:
choices: 30 days from receipt of the assessment
hints: The FLD/FAN is the 'assessment' that may be protested.
Supporting documents must follow within 60 days.
why: NIRC Sec. 228: the assessment (FLD/FAN) may be protested by a request for reconsideration or reinvestigation within 30 days from receipt; relevant supporting documents must be submitted within 60 days from filing the protest; otherwise, the assessment becomes final.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: A company received a PAN, answered it, and then received a Formal Letter of Demand with a Final Assessment Notice stating a definite due date. Believing that its answer to the PAN was enough, it did not file any protest against the FLD/FAN. Six months later, the BIR issued a warrant of distraint. Can the company still question the assessment?

alac.answer: No, the company can no longer question the assessment, which has become final.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC provides that the assessment may be protested administratively by filing a request for reconsideration or reinvestigation within thirty days from receipt of the assessment. The FLD/FAN is the assessment that must be protested; a reply to the PAN does not take its place. If no protest is filed within the period, the assessment becomes final, executory and demandable.
alac.application: Here, the company replied to the PAN but never protested the FLD/FAN within thirty days from receipt. The FLD/FAN, which states a definite due date, is a valid assessment that has become final.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company can no longer dispute the assessment, and the BIR may proceed with the distraint.

keyPoints: Protest of the FLD/FAN within 30 days (Sec. 228)
Reply to the PAN does not substitute for a protest
Unprotested assessment becomes final, executory and demandable
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: Under Section 222(a) of the NIRC, in case of a false or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax, or failure to file a return, the tax may be assessed within:
choices: Ten years after the discovery of the falsity, fraud or omission
Five years from the due date
hints: The ordinary period is three years (Sec. 203).
Fraud must be proved clearly; it is never presumed.
why: NIRC Sec. 203: the ordinary period to assess is three years from the last day for filing (or from actual filing if later); Sec. 222(a): ten years from discovery in case of false or fraudulent returns with intent to evade or failure to file. Fraud must be alleged and proved clearly; it is not presumed (CIR v. Javier, Jr., G.R. No. 78953, July 31, 1991).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 203 and 222; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Javier, Jr., G.R. No. 78953, July 31, 1991

q: A taxpayer filed his 2019 income tax return on April 15, 2020, but omitted some income through an honest mistake in classifying an item. In 2025, the BIR assessed him, claiming that the ten-year period applies because his return was "false." Is the assessment timely?

alac.answer: No, the assessment has prescribed because the return was not fraudulent.
alac.basis: Section 203 of the NIRC requires internal revenue taxes to be assessed within three years after the last day prescribed for filing the return. Section 222(a) extends the period to ten years from discovery only in the case of a false or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax, or failure to file a return. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Javier, Jr., G.R. No. 78953, July 31, 1991, the Supreme Court held that fraud is never presumed and must be clearly proved, and that a mere mistake or omission without intent to evade does not justify the ten-year period.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer filed his return on time, and the omission resulted from an honest mistake, without intent to evade. The three-year period applies, so the BIR had until April 15, 2023 to assess.
