alac.conclusion: Therefore, the 2025 assessment is barred by prescription.

keyPoints: Ordinary three-year period (Sec. 203)
Ten years only for false or fraudulent returns with intent to evade, or non-filing (Sec. 222(a))
Fraud must be clearly proved (CIR v. Javier)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 203 and 222; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Javier, Jr., G.R. No. 78953, July 31, 1991

q: Under Section 222(b) of the NIRC, the period to assess may be extended if:
choices: Before the three-year period expires, both the Commissioner and the taxpayer agree in writing to the assessment after that time
hints: A waiver must comply strictly with the rules (CIR v. Kudos Metal).
Sec. 223 lists grounds for suspension.
why: NIRC Sec. 222(b): the period may be extended by a written agreement (waiver) executed before its expiration; Sec. 223: the period is suspended, among others, when a reinvestigation requested by the taxpayer is granted or the taxpayer cannot be located. A defective waiver does not extend the period (CIR v. Kudos Metal Corporation, G.R. No. 178087, May 5, 2010).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 222 and 223; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Kudos Metal Corporation, G.R. No. 178087, May 5, 2010

q: To extend the period to assess its 2019 taxes, a company's accountant, without a board resolution or written authority, signed a waiver. The BIR's copy did not show when the BIR accepted it, and the company was not given its copy. The BIR then assessed the company after the original three-year period. Is the assessment timely?

alac.answer: No, the waiver is defective, so the assessment has prescribed.
alac.basis: Section 222(b) of the NIRC allows the period to assess to be extended if, before its expiration, both the Commissioner and the taxpayer agree in writing to the assessment after such time. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Kudos Metal Corporation, G.R. No. 178087, May 5, 2010, the Supreme Court held that a waiver of the statute of limitations must strictly comply with the requirements of the BIR rules, such as execution by the taxpayer's authorized representative, the date of acceptance by the BIR, and the furnishing of a copy to the taxpayer, and that a defective waiver does not extend the period.
alac.application: Here, the waiver was signed by an accountant without written authority from the company, did not show the date of the BIR's acceptance, and was not furnished to the company. These defects make the waiver invalid.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the period to assess was not extended, and the assessment issued after the three-year period is void for prescription.

keyPoints: Extension by written agreement before expiration (Sec. 222(b))
Strict compliance with waiver requirements (CIR v. Kudos Metal)
Defective waiver does not extend the period
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 222; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Kudos Metal Corporation, G.R. No. 178087, May 5, 2010

q: Before the BIR may collect a tax by distraint or levy, as a rule:
choices: There must be a valid assessment that has become final, executory and demandable, or an assessment made within the prescriptive period
A court must first convict the taxpayer
hints: Collection follows assessment.
Exception: collection without assessment in fraud or non-filing cases (Sec. 222(a)).
why: As a rule, collection requires a valid assessment issued within the prescriptive period and, for summary remedies, a final and demandable assessment; collection by court action without assessment is allowed only in cases under Sec. 222(a). Remedies are distraint and levy, or civil or criminal action (Sec. 205).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 205 and 222

q: The BIR issued a warrant of distraint against a taxpayer whose FAN was still under a timely protest pending before the CIR, and before the BIR had decided the protest. Is the distraint proper?

alac.answer: No, the distraint is premature because the assessment has not yet become final and demandable.
alac.basis: Section 205 of the NIRC provides the civil remedies for the collection of delinquent taxes, which presuppose a tax that is due and demandable. Under Section 228, a timely protested assessment does not become final, executory and demandable until the protest is decided and the decision becomes final, or the taxpayer fails to appeal within the period. Summary collection by distraint or levy generally requires a valid assessment that has become final.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer filed a timely protest, which the CIR had not yet decided. The assessment had not become final and demandable, so the taxpayer was not yet delinquent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the warrant of distraint was prematurely issued and may be set aside, unless the BIR shows grounds for constructive distraint to protect the government's interest.

keyPoints: Collection remedies for delinquent taxes (Sec. 205)
Timely protested assessment not yet final (Sec. 228)
Constructive distraint as a protective measure (Sec. 206)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 205, 206 and 228

q: Under Section 222(c) of the NIRC, a tax assessed within the prescriptive period may be collected by distraint or levy or by a court proceeding within:
choices: Five years following the assessment of the tax
hints: The period starts from the assessment.
A waiver may extend it if executed before expiration.
why: NIRC Sec. 222(c): a tax assessed within the period may be collected by distraint, levy or court proceeding within five years following the assessment; Sec. 222(d): the period may be extended by written agreement before it expires.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 222

q: The BIR validly assessed a taxpayer in March 2018. The taxpayer did not protest. The BIR did nothing until April 2024, when it filed a collection case and issued a warrant of levy. Is the collection timely?

alac.answer: No, the BIR's right to collect has prescribed.
alac.basis: Section 222(c) of the NIRC provides that any internal revenue tax which has been assessed within the period of limitation may be collected by distraint or levy or by a proceeding in court within five years following the assessment of the tax.
alac.application: Here, the tax was assessed in March 2018, so the BIR had until March 2023 to collect. It took no collection action until April 2024, more than five years later, and there is no showing of a written extension or suspension of the period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the collection case and the warrant of levy are barred by prescription.

keyPoints: Five years from assessment to collect (Sec. 222(c))
Extension only by written agreement before expiration (Sec. 222(d))
Late collection barred
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 222

q: Under Section 249(A) of the NIRC, as amended by the TRAIN law, the interest on any unpaid amount of tax is:
choices: Double the legal interest rate for loans or forbearance of money set by the BSP
hints: With the 6% legal rate, the interest is 12% a year.
Micro and small taxpayers get a 50% reduction under EOPT.
why: NIRC Sec. 249(A), as amended by RA 10963: interest at double the legal interest rate set by the BSP (currently 12% a year) on any unpaid tax; deficiency and delinquency interest are not imposed simultaneously. EOPT (RA 11976) Sec. 45 reduces the interest by 50% for micro and small taxpayers.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 249, as amended by RA 10963; Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976), Sec. 45

q: A micro taxpayer has an unpaid deficiency income tax. The BIR computed interest at 12% a year. The taxpayer argues that the interest should be lower. Is it correct?

alac.answer: Yes, the taxpayer is correct; as a micro taxpayer, it is entitled to a 50% reduction of the interest.
alac.basis: Section 249(A) of the NIRC, as amended by RA 10963, imposes interest on any unpaid amount of tax at double the legal interest rate for loans or forbearance of money set by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which is 12% a year at the current 6% legal rate. Section 45 of the Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976) grants micro and small taxpayers a fifty percent reduction on the interest rate imposed under Section 249.
alac.application: Here, the BIR applied the full 12% rate. But the taxpayer is a micro taxpayer under EOPT, so the interest rate should be reduced by half, to 6% a year.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the BIR should recompute the interest at the reduced rate for micro taxpayers.

keyPoints: Interest at double the legal rate (Sec. 249(A), as amended by TRAIN)
Currently 12% a year
50% reduction for micro and small taxpayers (RA 11976, Sec. 45)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 249, as amended by RA 10963; Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976), Sec. 45

q: Under Section 248(A) of the NIRC, a surcharge of 25% is imposed for, among others:
choices: Failure to file any return and pay the tax due on the date prescribed
hints: The surcharge is 50% for willful neglect to file or for a false or fraudulent return (Sec. 248(B)).
EOPT reduced the surcharge for micro and small taxpayers to 10%.
why: NIRC Sec. 248(A): a 25% surcharge applies for failure to file and pay on time, filing with the wrong officer (unless authorized), failure to pay a deficiency within the time in the notice, and failure to pay the full tax due; Sec. 248(B): 50% for willful neglect to file or a false or fraudulent return. RA 11976 Sec. 45: 10% for micro and small taxpayers.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 248; Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976), Sec. 45

q: A large corporation failed to pay a deficiency tax within the due date stated in its valid FAN. Separately, a small business owner filed his return and paid his tax one week late. What surcharges apply?

alac.answer: The corporation is liable for a 25% surcharge, and the small business owner is liable for a 10% surcharge.
alac.basis: Section 248(A) of the NIRC imposes, in addition to the tax, a penalty of twenty-five percent of the amount due for, among others, failure to file any return and pay the tax due on the date prescribed, and failure to pay the deficiency tax within the time prescribed in the notice of assessment. Section 45 of the Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976) grants micro and small taxpayers a reduced rate of ten percent for the civil penalties under Section 248.
alac.application: Here, the corporation failed to pay the deficiency tax within the due date in its FAN, so it incurs the 25% surcharge. The small business owner filed and paid late, which would normally incur 25%, but as a small taxpayer he is entitled to the reduced 10% rate.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation pays a 25% surcharge, while the small business owner pays a 10% surcharge, both in addition to interest.

keyPoints: 25% surcharge for late filing and payment or non-payment of a deficiency (Sec. 248(A))
50% for willful neglect or fraud (Sec. 248(B))
10% for micro and small taxpayers (RA 11976, Sec. 45)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 248; Ease of Paying Taxes Act (RA 11976), Sec. 45

q: A compromise penalty is:
choices: Mandatory and may be collected by distraint
An amount paid in lieu of criminal prosecution, which cannot be imposed or collected without the taxpayer's consent
hints: It is a settlement of a criminal violation.
The BIR cannot force it on the taxpayer.
why: A compromise penalty is a sum paid in lieu of criminal prosecution under NIRC Sec. 204(B); being a compromise, it requires the taxpayer's consent and cannot be collected by summary remedies or demanded by assessment. Criminal violations may be compromised except those already filed in court or involving fraud.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 204(B)

q: The BIR's FAN included a P25,000 "compromise penalty" for the taxpayer's late filing. The taxpayer protested, refusing to pay it. The BIR included it in its warrant of distraint. Is the BIR correct?

alac.answer: No, the BIR cannot collect the compromise penalty without the taxpayer's consent.
alac.basis: Section 204(B) of the NIRC allows the Commissioner to compromise criminal violations, except those already filed in court or involving fraud. A compromise penalty is an amount paid in lieu of criminal prosecution; as a compromise, it is a mutual agreement that requires the consent of the taxpayer. The BIR cannot impose it unilaterally, include it in an assessment as a demandable amount, or collect it through distraint.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer expressly refused to pay the compromise penalty. There is no agreement, so the BIR has no basis to collect it. Its remedy, if it believes a crime was committed, is to file a criminal case.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the compromise penalty should be removed from the warrant of distraint.

keyPoints: Compromise penalty is in lieu of criminal prosecution (Sec. 204(B))
Requires the taxpayer's consent
Cannot be collected by summary remedies
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 204

q: The period to protest a FAN/FLD under Section 228 of the NIRC is counted from:
choices: The end of the taxable year
The date the FAN was signed
The taxpayer's receipt of the assessment
hints: The period is 30 days.
Receipt must be proved by the BIR when denied.
why: NIRC Sec. 228: the protest (request for reconsideration or reinvestigation) must be filed within 30 days from receipt of the assessment; the BIR must prove receipt when the taxpayer denies it.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: A FAN was dated June 1 but was received by the taxpayer's authorized employee on June 20. The taxpayer filed its protest on July 15. The BIR says the protest is late because 30 days from June 1 had passed. Is the protest timely?

alac.answer: Yes, the protest is timely.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC provides that an assessment may be protested by filing a request for reconsideration or reinvestigation within thirty days from receipt of the assessment.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer received the FAN on June 20. The thirty-day period runs from that date, not from the date of the FAN, so it ends on July 20. The protest filed on July 15 is within the period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the protest was timely filed, and the assessment has not become final.

keyPoints: Protest within 30 days (Sec. 228)
Counted from receipt, not the date of the FAN
Timely protest prevents finality
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: If a taxpayer fails to protest an assessment within the period, the assessment:
choices: Becomes final, executory and demandable, and the taxpayer can no longer dispute its correctness
hints: Finality bars questions on the merits.
But a void assessment never becomes final.
why: Under NIRC Sec. 228, an assessment not protested on time becomes final, executory and demandable; the taxpayer may no longer question its correctness in a collection case, unless the assessment is void (e.g., issued without due process).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: A taxpayer did not protest a valid FAN. When the BIR filed a collection case two years later, the taxpayer raised for the first time that the assessed income was not his. Can he still raise this defense?

alac.answer: No, he can no longer dispute the correctness of the assessment.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC provides that an assessment may be protested within thirty days from receipt; otherwise, the assessment becomes final, executory and demandable. Once final, the assessment can no longer be questioned on the merits in a collection proceeding, and the court will enforce it, unless the assessment itself is void.
alac.application: Here, the FAN was valid, and the taxpayer did not protest it. It became final, executory and demandable. His claim that the income was not his goes to the merits of the assessment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he can no longer raise that defense, and the BIR may collect the tax.

keyPoints: Unprotested assessment becomes final (Sec. 228)
Merits can no longer be questioned in collection
Exception: void assessments
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: Under Section 228 of the NIRC, after filing a protest, the taxpayer must submit all relevant supporting documents within:
choices: 60 days from filing of the protest
hints: The taxpayer determines which documents are relevant.
The 180-day period for the CIR runs from submission.
why: NIRC Sec. 228: within 60 days from filing of the protest, all relevant supporting documents shall have been submitted, otherwise the assessment becomes final; the taxpayer, not the BIR, determines what documents are relevant (CIR v. First Express Pawnshop Company, Inc., G.R. Nos. 172045-46, June 16, 2009).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. First Express Pawnshop Company, Inc., G.R. Nos. 172045-46, June 16, 2009

q: A taxpayer filed a timely protest and, within 60 days, submitted the documents it considered relevant. The BIR later said that the taxpayer should have submitted additional documents it never asked for, and that the assessment had therefore become final. Is the BIR correct?

alac.answer: No, the BIR is not correct.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC requires that, within sixty days from filing of the protest, all relevant supporting documents shall have been submitted; otherwise, the assessment becomes final. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. First Express Pawnshop Company, Inc., G.R. Nos. 172045-46, June 16, 2009, the Supreme Court held that the term "relevant supporting documents" refers to the documents the taxpayer believes necessary to support its protest, and that the BIR cannot demand what documents the taxpayer must submit in order to make the assessment final.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer submitted within sixty days the documents it considered relevant. The BIR's later claim that other documents were needed does not make the assessment final.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the assessment did not become final, and the BIR must decide the protest on the documents submitted.

keyPoints: Supporting documents within 60 days from protest (Sec. 228)
The taxpayer determines relevant documents (CIR v. First Express Pawnshop)
Assessment does not become final
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. First Express Pawnshop Company, Inc., G.R. Nos. 172045-46, June 16, 2009

q: Under Section 228 of the NIRC, the Commissioner must act on a protest within:
hints: If the CIR does not act, the taxpayer has options.
The period runs from submission of the supporting documents.
why: NIRC Sec. 228: if the protest is denied or not acted upon within 180 days from submission of documents, the taxpayer may appeal to the CTA within 30 days from receipt of the decision or from the lapse of the 180-day period.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: A taxpayer filed a protest on March 1 and submitted its supporting documents on April 15. As of October 20, the CIR had not acted. When did the 180-day period begin and end, and what may the taxpayer do now?

alac.answer: The 180 days ran from April 15 and ended about October 12; the taxpayer may appeal to the CTA within 30 days from that date, or wait for the CIR's decision.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC provides that if the protest is not acted upon within one hundred eighty days from submission of documents, the taxpayer adversely affected may appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals within thirty days from the lapse of the one hundred eighty-day period. In Lascona Land Co., Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 171251, March 5, 2012, the Supreme Court held that, in case of inaction, the taxpayer may either appeal to the CTA within thirty days after the 180-day period, or await the final decision of the CIR and appeal it within thirty days from receipt.
alac.application: Here, the 180 days are counted from the submission of documents on April 15, not from the protest on March 1, so the period ended around October 12. As of October 20, the taxpayer is still within the thirty days to appeal the inaction, or it may choose to wait for the CIR's decision.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the taxpayer may file a petition for review with the CTA by about November 11, or await the CIR's decision and appeal within thirty days from receiving it.

keyPoints: CIR acts within 180 days from submission of documents (Sec. 228)
Appeal within 30 days from lapse of 180 days
Option to wait for the decision (Lascona Land v. CIR)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Lascona Land Co., Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 171251, March 5, 2012

q: If the CIR denies a protest, the taxpayer's remedy under Section 228 of the NIRC is to:
choices: Appeal to the Secretary of Justice
Appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals within 30 days from receipt of the decision
File a case in the RTC
hints: The CTA has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over CIR decisions on disputed assessments.
A motion for reconsideration with the CIR does not stop the 30 days.
why: NIRC Sec. 228 and RA 9282 Sec. 7(a)(1)-(2): the taxpayer may appeal the CIR's denial, or inaction after 180 days, to the CTA within 30 days. Under Lascona Land Co., Inc. v. CIR, G.R. No. 171251, March 5, 2012, in case of inaction the taxpayer may appeal or await the decision.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228; Lascona Land Co., Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 171251, March 5, 2012

q: The CIR denied a taxpayer's protest in a letter received on May 2, stating that it was the CIR's final decision. On May 20, the taxpayer filed a motion for reconsideration with the CIR, which was denied on July 1. The taxpayer appealed to the CTA on July 25. Is the appeal timely?

alac.answer: No, the appeal was filed out of time.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC provides that if the protest is denied, the taxpayer adversely affected may appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals within thirty days from receipt of the decision; otherwise, the decision shall become final, executory and demandable. RA 9282 likewise requires the appeal within thirty days from receipt. A motion for reconsideration of the CIR's final decision on the disputed assessment does not toll the thirty-day period.
alac.application: Here, the CIR's final decision was received on May 2, so the taxpayer had until June 1 to appeal to the CTA. Its motion for reconsideration with the CIR did not suspend the period, so the appeal filed on July 25 was late.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CTA should dismiss the appeal, and the CIR's decision has become final.

keyPoints: Appeal to the CTA within 30 days from receipt of the denial (Sec. 228)
Motion for reconsideration with the CIR does not toll the period
Late appeal: decision becomes final
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: If the taxpayer fails to appeal the CIR's denial of its protest to the CTA within 30 days:
choices: The decision becomes final, executory and demandable
The taxpayer may file in the RTC
hints: Finality follows failure to appeal.
Collection may proceed.
why: NIRC Sec. 228: failure to appeal the CIR's decision within 30 days makes it final, executory and demandable, and the BIR may proceed with collection.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: A taxpayer did not appeal the CIR's final decision denying its protest. Months later, when the BIR levied on its properties, it filed a petition with the CTA questioning the merits of the assessment. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: No, the petition will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 228 of the NIRC provides that the taxpayer adversely affected by the decision of the CIR may appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals within thirty days from receipt of the decision; otherwise, the decision shall become final, executory and demandable. Once final, the assessment may be enforced by the BIR's collection remedies, and its merits can no longer be reviewed.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer did not appeal the CIR's decision within thirty days. The decision became final, executory and demandable, and the BIR properly levied on its properties.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CTA petition questioning the merits of the assessment should be dismissed.

keyPoints: Failure to appeal within 30 days makes the decision final (Sec. 228)
BIR may enforce collection
Merits no longer reviewable
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: Under Section 253(a) of the NIRC, payment of the tax due after apprehension:
choices: Shall not constitute a valid defense in any prosecution for violation of the Code
hints: Criminal violations may be compromised before filing in court, except fraud cases (Sec. 204(B)).
Payment after apprehension is not a defense.
why: NIRC Sec. 204(B): criminal violations may be compromised, except those already filed in court or involving fraud; Sec. 253(a): payment of the tax due after apprehension shall not constitute a valid defense in any prosecution.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 204 and 253

q: A taxpayer charged in court with willful failure to file returns offered to pay all his deficiency taxes and to compromise the criminal case. Separately, another taxpayer under investigation, not yet charged, offered to compromise a non-fraudulent failure to file. Rule on both.

alac.answer: The first taxpayer's case can no longer be compromised, and his payment is not a defense; the second taxpayer's violation may be compromised.
alac.basis: Section 204(B) of the NIRC provides that all criminal violations may be compromised except (a) those already filed in court, or (b) those involving fraud. Section 253(a) provides that payment of the tax due after apprehension shall not constitute a valid defense in any prosecution for violation of any provision of the Code.
alac.application: Here, the first taxpayer's case is already filed in court, so it cannot be compromised, and his payment of the deficiency taxes after apprehension is not a defense, though it settles his civil liability. The second taxpayer has not been charged, and his violation does not involve fraud, so the CIR may accept a compromise.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the first criminal case must proceed, while the second violation may be settled by compromise.

keyPoints: Compromise of criminal violations except those filed in court or involving fraud (Sec. 204(B))
Payment after apprehension is not a defense (Sec. 253(a))
Civil liability still settled by payment
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 204 and 253

q: Under Sections 204(C) and 229 of the NIRC, a claim for refund of taxes erroneously or illegally collected must be filed within:
choices: Two years after the payment of the tax or penalty
hints: Both the administrative claim and the court action must be within two years.
A return showing overpayment counts as a written claim.
why: NIRC Secs. 204(C) and 229: a written claim for refund must be filed with the CIR, and the suit in court must also be filed, within two years after payment, regardless of supervening causes; a return showing an overpayment is considered a written claim. Under RA 11976, the CIR decides within 180 days.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 204(C) and 229

q: A corporation paid P5 million in income tax on April 15, 2023, later discovering that part of it was not due. It filed a written refund claim with the BIR on March 1, 2025. The BIR did not act, and on May 2, 2025, the corporation filed a case with the CTA. Is the judicial claim timely?

alac.answer: No, the judicial claim is late; it should have been filed by April 15, 2025.
alac.basis: Section 229 of the NIRC provides that no suit or proceeding shall be maintained in any court for the recovery of any tax alleged to have been erroneously or illegally collected until a claim for refund has been duly filed with the Commissioner, and that no such suit or proceeding shall be filed after the expiration of two years from the date of payment of the tax. Both the administrative and judicial claims must be filed within the two-year period.
alac.application: Here, the tax was paid on April 15, 2023, so the two-year period ended on April 15, 2025. The administrative claim on March 1, 2025 was timely, but the CTA case filed on May 2, 2025 was beyond the period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CTA should dismiss the judicial claim for having been filed out of time.

keyPoints: Administrative claim required before court action (Sec. 229)
Both claims within two years from payment
Late judicial claim barred
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 229

q: For refunds of erroneously paid national taxes (other than VAT input tax), which statement is correct?
choices: The taxpayer may go to court first
Only an administrative claim is needed
The judicial claim may be filed any time after the CIR acts
An administrative claim must first be filed with the CIR, and the judicial claim must be filed within two years from payment, even if the CIR has not yet acted
hints: The two-year period is not suspended by the pending administrative claim.
VAT input tax refunds follow Sec. 112 instead.
why: Under NIRC Sec. 229 (and Sec. 204(C)), the administrative claim is a condition precedent to the judicial claim, and both must be filed within two years from payment; the taxpayer should go to court before the two years lapse even if the CIR has not acted (CIR v. Philippine American Life Insurance Co., G.R. No. 105208, May 29, 1995). VAT input tax refunds follow Sec. 112.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 229; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine American Life Insurance Co., G.R. No. 105208, May 29, 1995

q: A taxpayer paid excess income tax and filed a refund claim with the BIR within the two-year period. The BIR did not act. The taxpayer waited for a decision and did not go to court, and the two years lapsed. When the BIR finally denied the claim, the taxpayer appealed to the CTA. Will the CTA grant the refund?

alac.answer: No, the judicial claim is barred because it was not filed within two years from payment.
alac.basis: Section 229 of the NIRC requires that a claim for refund be duly filed with the Commissioner before a suit is filed, and that no suit shall be filed after the expiration of two years from the date of payment of the tax, regardless of any supervening cause. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine American Life Insurance Co., G.R. No. 105208, May 29, 1995, the Supreme Court held that the two-year period applies to both the administrative and the judicial claims, so the taxpayer must file the court case within the period even if the CIR has not yet acted on the administrative claim.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer's administrative claim was timely, but it waited for the BIR's action and let the two years lapse before going to court. The pendency of the administrative claim did not suspend the period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CTA cannot grant the refund.

keyPoints: Administrative claim is a condition for the judicial claim (Sec. 229)
Both within two years from payment
Pending administrative claim does not suspend the period (CIR v. Philamlife)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 229; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Philippine American Life Insurance Co., G.R. No. 105208, May 29, 1995

q: Who is the proper party to claim a refund of an indirect tax, such as VAT or excise tax passed on to the buyer?
choices: The statutory taxpayer who paid the tax to the government
The buyer who bore the burden
The withholding agent of the buyer
hints: The buyer pays part of the price, not a tax.
A withholding agent may claim refund of tax it withheld and remitted (CIR v. Procter & Gamble).
why: The proper party to claim a refund of indirect taxes is the statutory taxpayer, the person on whom the tax is imposed by law (Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. CIR, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008). For withholding taxes, the withholding agent may file the claim (CIR v. Procter & Gamble Philippine Manufacturing Corporation, G.R. No. L-66838, December 2, 1991).
cite: Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Procter & Gamble Philippine Manufacturing Corporation, G.R. No. L-66838, December 2, 1991

q: A Philippine subsidiary withheld and remitted the final tax on dividends paid to its foreign parent at the regular rate, though a lower rate applied. The subsidiary filed the claim for refund of the excess in its own name. The CIR argues that only the foreign parent, the taxpayer, may claim the refund. Who is correct?

alac.answer: The subsidiary may file the claim as withholding agent.
alac.basis: In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Procter & Gamble Philippine Manufacturing Corporation, G.R. No. L-66838, December 2, 1991, the Supreme Court held that a withholding agent which withheld and remitted the tax on dividends to its foreign parent is a proper party to claim the refund, because it is directly and independently liable for the correct amount of the tax as withholding agent, and the refund benefits the taxpayer. This differs from indirect taxes, where only the statutory taxpayer may claim (Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008).
alac.application: Here, the subsidiary, as withholding agent, withheld and remitted the excess tax on the dividends. It is liable for the correct amount of the withholding tax, so it has a real interest in the refund of the excess.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the subsidiary may claim the refund, which it holds for the benefit of the foreign parent.

keyPoints: Withholding agent may claim refund of excess withheld (CIR v. Procter & Gamble)
Agent is directly liable for correct withholding
Indirect taxes: only the statutory taxpayer (Silkair v. CIR)
cite: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Procter & Gamble Philippine Manufacturing Corporation, G.R. No. L-66838, December 2, 1991; Silkair (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 173594, February 6, 2008

q: Under Section 219 of the NIRC, the tax lien in favor of the government attaches:
choices: From the time the assessment was made by the Commissioner, upon the taxpayer's neglect or refusal to pay after demand
From the filing of the return
hints: The lien covers all property and rights to property.
It is not valid against certain third parties until notice is filed with the Register of Deeds.
why: NIRC Sec. 219: if a person liable to pay a tax neglects or refuses to pay after demand, the amount is a lien in favor of the government from the time the assessment was made, until paid, on all property and rights to property of the taxpayer, but it is not valid against a mortgagee, purchaser or judgment creditor until notice is filed with the Register of Deeds.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 219

q: The BIR assessed Lito in January and demanded payment, which he refused. In March, he sold his land to Mara, a buyer in good faith, before the BIR filed any notice of the tax lien with the Register of Deeds. Can the BIR enforce the tax lien against the land in Mara's hands?

alac.answer: No, the lien is not valid against Mara, a good-faith purchaser, because no notice was filed before the sale.
alac.basis: Section 219 of the NIRC provides that when a taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay a tax after demand, the amount shall be a lien in favor of the government from the time when the assessment was made, upon all property and rights to property belonging to the taxpayer, but that the lien shall not be valid against any mortgagee, purchaser or judgment creditor until notice of such lien shall be filed by the Commissioner in the office of the Register of Deeds.
alac.application: Here, a lien arose in favor of the government when Lito refused to pay after the assessment and demand. But the BIR filed no notice with the Register of Deeds before Lito sold the land to Mara, a purchaser in good faith.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the BIR cannot enforce the lien against the land in Mara's hands, though it may pursue Lito's other properties.

keyPoints: Tax lien from the time of assessment upon refusal to pay after demand (Sec. 219)
Covers all property and rights of the taxpayer
Not valid against purchasers until notice is filed with the Register of Deeds
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 219

q: Under Section 206 of the NIRC, constructive distraint may be placed on the property of:
choices: A delinquent taxpayer, or a taxpayer who, in the CIR's opinion, is retiring from business, intending to leave the Philippines, or hiding his property
hints: Actual distraint seizes property; constructive distraint only prohibits its disposal.
Distraint applies to personal property; levy to real property.
why: NIRC Sec. 205: civil remedies include distraint of personal property and levy upon real property; Sec. 206: to safeguard government interests, the CIR may place under constructive distraint the property of a delinquent taxpayer or one who is retiring from business, leaving the Philippines, or concealing property, by requiring him not to dispose of it.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 205-207

q: A foreign businessman under BIR audit, but not yet assessed, began transferring his assets abroad and booked a one-way flight out of the country. The CIR placed his cars and bank accounts under constructive distraint. He argues that he is not yet delinquent. Is the constructive distraint valid?

alac.answer: Yes, the constructive distraint is valid.
alac.basis: Section 206 of the NIRC provides that, to safeguard the interest of the government, the Commissioner may place under constructive distraint the property of a delinquent taxpayer or any taxpayer who, in his opinion, is retiring from any business subject to tax, or is intending to leave the Philippines or to remove his property therefrom or to hide or conceal his property. Constructive distraint does not seize the property but requires the taxpayer not to dispose of it without the CIR's consent.
alac.application: Here, although the businessman is not yet delinquent, he is moving his assets abroad and is intending to leave the Philippines. These are express grounds for constructive distraint, which may be imposed even before an assessment becomes final.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CIR validly placed his property under constructive distraint to protect the government's interest.

keyPoints: Constructive distraint to safeguard government interest (Sec. 206)
Grounds include intent to leave the Philippines and removing property
Available even if the taxpayer is not yet delinquent
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 205 and 206

q: Under Section 215 of the NIRC, if there is no bidder at the auction of real property levied for taxes, or the highest bid is insufficient:
choices: The property is returned to the taxpayer
The property is declared forfeited to the government in satisfaction of the claim
The BIR must buy it at market value
hints: The taxpayer has a right of redemption (Sec. 214).
The forfeiture is recorded with the Register of Deeds.
why: NIRC Sec. 215: if there is no bidder for levied real property, or the highest bid is insufficient to pay the taxes, penalties and costs, the revenue officer shall declare the property forfeited to the government; the taxpayer may redeem within one year (Sec. 214).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 214 and 215

q: The BIR levied on a delinquent taxpayer's lot and auctioned it, but the only bid was far below the taxes owed. What may the revenue officer do, and does the taxpayer have any remedy?

alac.answer: The revenue officer may declare the lot forfeited to the government, and the taxpayer may still redeem it within one year.
alac.basis: Section 215 of the NIRC provides that in case there is no bidder for real property exposed for sale, or if the highest bid is for an amount insufficient to pay the taxes, penalties and costs, the Internal Revenue Officer conducting the sale shall declare the property forfeited to the government in satisfaction of the claim. Section 214 gives the delinquent taxpayer the right to redeem the property within one year from the date of sale or forfeiture, by paying the amount of the taxes, penalties, interest and costs.
alac.application: Here, the only bid was insufficient to pay the taxes owed. The revenue officer may therefore declare the lot forfeited to the government, and the forfeiture must be recorded with the Register of Deeds.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the lot may be forfeited, but the taxpayer has one year to redeem it by paying the full amount due.

keyPoints: Forfeiture for want of bidder or insufficient bid (Sec. 215)
Recorded with the Register of Deeds
Right of redemption within one year (Sec. 214)
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 214 and 215

q: Under Section 115 of the NIRC, the Commissioner may suspend the business operations of a VAT-registered person for:
choices: Failure to issue receipts or invoices, failure to file a VAT return, or understatement of taxable sales by 30% or more
hints: This is an administrative remedy.
Failure to register is also a ground.
why: NIRC Sec. 115: the CIR may suspend business operations and temporarily close the establishment of a VAT-registered person for failure to issue receipts or invoices, failure to file a VAT return, or understatement of taxable sales by 30% or more; also for failure of any person to register.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 115

q: BIR test-buyers found that a VAT-registered restaurant repeatedly failed to issue receipts. The BIR ordered the restaurant closed for at least five days. The owner argues that only a court may close a business. Is the closure valid?

alac.answer: Yes, the closure is valid.
alac.basis: Section 115 of the NIRC empowers the Commissioner or his authorized representative to suspend the business operations and temporarily close the business establishment of any person for, among others, failure of a VAT-registered person to issue receipts or invoices. This is an administrative remedy that does not require a court order, though the taxpayer must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard under the BIR's rules.
alac.application: Here, the restaurant is VAT-registered and repeatedly failed to issue receipts, as shown by the test-buyers. That is an express ground for suspension and temporary closure by the CIR.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the BIR may validly close the restaurant temporarily, without a court order, after complying with the required notice.

keyPoints: Suspension of business operations (Sec. 115)
Ground: failure of a VAT-registered person to issue receipts
Administrative remedy, no court order needed
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 115

q: Under Section 220 of the NIRC, a civil action for the collection of taxes:
choices: Must be filed by the taxpayer
Shall be brought in the name of the Government of the Philippines, conducted by BIR legal officers, and filed only with the approval of the Commissioner
May be filed by any BIR employee without approval
hints: Civil and criminal actions are judicial remedies (Sec. 205(b)).
Jurisdiction depends on the amount (RA 9282).
why: NIRC Sec. 220: civil and criminal actions shall be brought in the name of the Government, conducted by BIR legal officers, and filed with the Commissioner's approval; Sec. 205: administrative and judicial remedies may be pursued simultaneously. Collection cases of P1 million or more are filed with the CTA (RA 9282, Sec. 7(c)).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Secs. 205 and 220

q: A revenue district officer, without the CIR's approval, filed a civil action in the RTC to collect P800,000 in final and executory deficiency taxes. Is the action properly filed?

alac.answer: No, the action was improperly filed because it lacked the Commissioner's approval.
alac.basis: Section 220 of the NIRC provides that civil and criminal actions instituted on behalf of the government shall be brought in the name of the Government of the Philippines, shall be conducted by legal officers of the BIR, and that no civil or criminal action for the recovery of taxes shall be filed in court without the approval of the Commissioner. Under RA 9282, collection cases involving less than P1 million are tried by the regular courts.
alac.application: Here, the amount of P800,000 is below P1 million, so the RTC (or the proper first-level court, depending on the amount) has jurisdiction rather than the CTA. But the revenue district officer filed the case without the Commissioner's approval, as Section 220 requires.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the action is defective and may be dismissed, without prejudice to its refiling with the Commissioner's approval within the prescriptive period.

keyPoints: Civil action in the name of the Government, with the CIR's approval (Sec. 220)
Below P1 million: regular courts (RA 9282)
Lack of approval is fatal
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 220; RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(c)

q: In Ungab v. Cusi, the Supreme Court held that a criminal prosecution for tax evasion:
choices: May proceed even without a prior assessment, because the crime is complete when the taxpayer knowingly files a fraudulent return
Is barred by a pending protest
hints: Assessment is not a prerequisite to a criminal case.
Criminal and civil remedies are separate.
why: A criminal action for tax evasion does not require a prior assessment; the crime is complete when the taxpayer knowingly and willfully files a fraudulent return with intent to evade (Ungab v. Cusi, G.R. Nos. L-41919-24, May 30, 1980). NIRC Sec. 221: penalties are enforced by criminal or civil action with the CIR's approval.
cite: Ungab v. Cusi, G.R. Nos. L-41919-24, May 30, 1980; National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 221

q: The BIR filed criminal complaints for tax evasion against a businessman for filing fraudulent income tax returns. He moved to dismiss, arguing that there is no final assessment yet and that his protest of a related assessment is pending. Should the case be dismissed?

alac.answer: No, the criminal case should not be dismissed.
alac.basis: In Ungab v. Cusi, G.R. Nos. L-41919-24, May 30, 1980, the Supreme Court held that an assessment of the tax deficiency is not necessary before a criminal prosecution for tax evasion may proceed, because the crime is complete when the violator has knowingly and willfully filed a fraudulent return with intent to evade the tax, and that a pending protest or request for reinvestigation does not bar the criminal case. Section 221 of the NIRC provides that statutory penalties are enforced by criminal or civil action, subject to the approval of the Commissioner.
alac.application: Here, the charge is for filing fraudulent returns. The crime was complete when the businessman knowingly filed those returns. The absence of a final assessment and the pendency of his protest do not affect the criminal action.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the motion to dismiss should be denied, and the criminal case may proceed.

keyPoints: No prior assessment needed for tax evasion prosecution (Ungab v. Cusi)
Crime complete upon knowingly filing a fraudulent return
Pending protest does not bar the case
cite: Ungab v. Cusi, G.R. Nos. L-41919-24, May 30, 1980; National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 221

q: Under Section 7(a) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, the CTA has exclusive appellate jurisdiction to review by appeal:
choices: Decisions or inaction of the CIR in disputed assessments, refunds and other matters under the NIRC; RTC decisions in local tax cases; Customs decisions; and CBAA decisions, among others
hints: The CTA also has original jurisdiction in collection cases of P1 million or more (Sec. 7(c)).
Inaction of the CIR is appealable.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 7(a): the CTA has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions and inaction of the CIR in disputed assessments and refunds; RTC decisions in local tax cases; decisions of the Commissioner of Customs; CBAA decisions; and certain decisions of the Secretaries of Finance, Trade and Agriculture. Sec. 7(c): original jurisdiction over collection cases of P1 million or more.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7

q: A taxpayer wants to challenge (a) the CIR's denial of its protest of a deficiency income tax assessment, and (b) an RTC decision upholding a city's business tax assessment against it. Which court should hear each, and how?

alac.answer: Both go to the CTA: the first by petition for review of the CIR's decision, and the second by appeal from the RTC's decision in a local tax case.
alac.basis: Section 7(a) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, gives the CTA exclusive appellate jurisdiction to review by appeal (1) decisions of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue in cases involving disputed assessments and (3) decisions, orders or resolutions of the Regional Trial Courts in local tax cases originally decided or resolved by them in the exercise of their original or appellate jurisdiction. Section 11 requires the appeal within thirty days from receipt of the decision, by petition for review.
alac.application: Here, the CIR's denial of the protest is a decision in a disputed assessment case, appealable to the CTA. The RTC's decision on the city's business tax assessment is a decision in a local tax case, also appealable to the CTA.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the taxpayer should file petitions for review with the CTA within thirty days from receipt of each decision.

keyPoints: CTA appellate jurisdiction over CIR decisions on disputed assessments (Sec. 7(a)(1))
Over RTC decisions in local tax cases (Sec. 7(a)(3))
Petition for review within 30 days (Sec. 11)
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Secs. 7 and 11

q: Under Section 7(b) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, criminal offenses arising from violations of the NIRC where the principal amount of taxes claimed is less than P1 million are tried by:
choices: The regular courts, with the CTA having appellate jurisdiction
hints: P1 million or more: CTA original jurisdiction.
The civil action is deemed jointly instituted.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 7(b): the CTA has exclusive original jurisdiction over criminal offenses under the NIRC and customs laws, but those where the principal amount is less than P1 million, or where no amount is specified, are tried by the regular courts, with the CTA exercising appellate jurisdiction.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)

q: Two criminal cases for willful failure to pay taxes were filed: one involving P5 million in principal taxes, the other P400,000. Where should each be filed, and where does an appeal go?

alac.answer: The P5 million case is filed with the CTA; the P400,000 case is filed with the regular courts, appealable to the CTA.
alac.basis: Section 7(b) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that the CTA has exclusive original jurisdiction over all criminal offenses arising from violations of the NIRC, but offenses where the principal amount of taxes and fees, exclusive of charges and penalties, claimed is less than P1,000,000 or where there is no specified amount shall be tried by the regular courts, and the jurisdiction of the CTA shall be appellate.
alac.application: Here, the first case involves P5 million in principal taxes, so it falls within the CTA's exclusive original jurisdiction, heard by a Division. The second involves P400,000, below the threshold, so it is tried by the regular courts, and the CTA has appellate jurisdiction over the decision.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the P5 million case goes to the CTA, and the P400,000 case goes to the regular court, with appeal to the CTA.

keyPoints: CTA original jurisdiction over tax crimes of P1 million or more (Sec. 7(b))
Below P1 million: regular courts
CTA appellate jurisdiction over those
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)

q: In City of Manila v. Grecia-Cuerdo, the Supreme Court held that the CTA has jurisdiction over:
choices: Petitions for certiorari questioning interlocutory orders of the RTC in local tax cases, in aid of its appellate jurisdiction
hints: The CTA's appellate power implies certiorari power over the same cases.
This avoids split jurisdiction.
why: The CTA has jurisdiction over petitions for certiorari assailing interlocutory orders of the RTC in local tax cases, because its appellate jurisdiction over those cases includes the power to issue writs necessary in aid of it (City of Manila v. Grecia-Cuerdo, G.R. No. 175723, February 4, 2014).
cite: City of Manila v. Grecia-Cuerdo, G.R. No. 175723, February 4, 2014

q: In a local tax refund case, the RTC issued a writ of preliminary injunction stopping a city from collecting business taxes. The city wants to challenge the interlocutory order by certiorari. Should it file with the Court of Appeals or the CTA?

alac.answer: The city should file the petition for certiorari with the CTA.
alac.basis: Section 7(a)(3) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, gives the CTA exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions of the RTC in local tax cases. In City of Manila v. Grecia-Cuerdo, G.R. No. 175723, February 4, 2014, the Supreme Court held that the CTA has jurisdiction over a special civil action for certiorari questioning an interlocutory order of the RTC in a local tax case, because the authority to issue writs of certiorari in aid of its appellate jurisdiction is included in that appellate jurisdiction, and splitting jurisdiction between the CA and the CTA is abhorred.
alac.application: Here, the RTC's writ of preliminary injunction is an interlocutory order in a local tax case, which falls within the CTA's appellate jurisdiction.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the city should file its petition for certiorari with the CTA, not the Court of Appeals.

keyPoints: CTA appellate jurisdiction over RTC local tax cases (Sec. 7(a)(3))
Certiorari in aid of appellate jurisdiction (City of Manila v. Grecia-Cuerdo)
No splitting of jurisdiction
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(a)(3); City of Manila v. Grecia-Cuerdo, G.R. No. 175723, February 4, 2014

q: Under Section 7(c) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, the CTA has exclusive original jurisdiction over tax collection cases involving final and executory assessments where the principal amount is:
choices: P1 million or more; below that, the proper MTC, MeTC or RTC tries the case
hints: The assessment must already be final and executory.
The CTA is appellate for collection cases tried by RTCs.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 7(c): the CTA has exclusive original jurisdiction over collection cases involving final and executory assessments where the principal amount is P1 million or more; cases below P1 million are tried by the proper first-level courts or RTCs, with the CTA exercising appellate jurisdiction over RTC decisions.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(c)

q: The BIR wants to file a civil action to collect P3 million in deficiency taxes from a taxpayer whose assessment became final when he failed to protest. Where should it file, and may the taxpayer question the assessment there?

alac.answer: The BIR should file with the CTA, and the taxpayer can no longer question the correctness of the final assessment.
alac.basis: Section 7(c) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, gives the CTA exclusive original jurisdiction in tax collection cases involving final and executory assessments, except those where the principal amount claimed is less than P1,000,000, which are tried by the proper first-level courts or RTCs. Section 228 of the NIRC makes an unprotested assessment final, executory and demandable.
alac.application: Here, the assessment is final and executory because the taxpayer did not protest, and the principal amount is P3 million, above the P1 million threshold. The collection case therefore belongs to the CTA's exclusive original jurisdiction.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the BIR should file the case with the CTA, where the taxpayer may no longer dispute the merits of the assessment.

keyPoints: CTA original jurisdiction in collection cases of P1 million or more (Sec. 7(c))
Final and executory assessment required
Merits no longer open to question
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(c); National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 228

q: Where is a judicial action to collect delinquent local taxes filed?
choices: In the regular courts with jurisdiction over the amount (first-level courts or the RTC), with appeal from the RTC to the CTA
hints: LGU judicial remedies are under LGC Sec. 174(b).
The CTA reviews RTC decisions in local tax cases.
why: Local tax collection cases are filed by the LGU in the regular courts with jurisdiction over the amount (LGC Sec. 174(b)); the CTA has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over RTC decisions in local tax cases (RA 9282, Sec. 7(a)(3)).
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(a)(3); Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 174

q: A city filed a collection case for P2.5 million in delinquent business taxes in the RTC. The taxpayer moved to dismiss, arguing that collection cases above P1 million belong to the CTA. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, the taxpayer is not correct; the RTC has jurisdiction over the local tax collection case.
alac.basis: Section 7(c) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, gives the CTA original jurisdiction over collection cases involving final and executory assessments for national internal revenue and customs taxes; it does not give the CTA original jurisdiction over local tax collection cases. Under the Local Government Code (Section 174), LGUs collect delinquent local taxes by judicial action in the regular courts, and Section 7(a)(3) of RA 1125, as amended, gives the CTA exclusive appellate jurisdiction over RTC decisions in local tax cases.
alac.application: Here, the city is collecting local business taxes, not national internal revenue taxes. The case is properly filed in the RTC, which has jurisdiction based on the amount, and any appeal from the RTC's decision goes to the CTA.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the motion to dismiss should be denied.

keyPoints: CTA original jurisdiction in collection cases covers national taxes (Sec. 7(c))
Local tax collection cases are filed in regular courts (LGC Sec. 174)
CTA appellate jurisdiction over RTC local tax decisions (Sec. 7(a)(3))
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7; Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), Sec. 174

q: Under Section 11 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, a party adversely affected by a decision of the CIR may appeal to the CTA:
choices: Within 15 days by notice of appeal
Within 30 days after receipt of the decision, or after the expiration of the period fixed by law for action, by filing a petition for review
hints: The petition is analogous to Rule 42.
A CTA Division hears the appeal.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 11: any party adversely affected by a decision, ruling or inaction of the CIR, Customs, the Secretaries, the CBAA or the RTC may appeal to the CTA within 30 days after receipt of the decision or after the expiration of the period for action, by petition for review analogous to Rule 42; the appeal does not suspend collection unless the CTA so orders.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 11

q: A taxpayer received the CIR's decision denying its refund claim on June 1. On June 25, it filed a notice of appeal with the CTA, without a petition for review, believing that the appeal would automatically stop the BIR's collection of a related deficiency assessment. Was the appeal properly made, and does it suspend collection?

alac.answer: The appeal should have been made by petition for review, and it does not automatically suspend collection.
alac.basis: Section 11 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that any party adversely affected by a decision of the CIR may appeal to the CTA within thirty days after receipt, and that the appeal shall be made by filing a petition for review under a procedure analogous to Rule 42 of the Rules of Civil Procedure. It also provides that no appeal taken to the CTA shall suspend the payment, levy, distraint, or sale of any property of the taxpayer, unless the CTA so orders.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer filed within thirty days, but by notice of appeal instead of a petition for review, which is the required mode. In any case, the appeal does not automatically suspend the BIR's collection; the taxpayer must ask the CTA to suspend it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the taxpayer should file a proper petition for review within the period and, if needed, move the CTA to suspend collection.

keyPoints: Appeal within 30 days (Sec. 11)
Mode: petition for review analogous to Rule 42
Appeal does not suspend collection unless the CTA orders
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 11

q: Under Section 11 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, the CTA may suspend the collection of a tax when collection may jeopardize the interest of the government and/or the taxpayer, and may require the taxpayer to:
choices: Deposit the amount claimed or file a surety bond for not more than double the amount
hints: The rule is no suspension; this is the exception.
The bond may be dispensed with in proper cases (e.g., void assessments).
why: RA 9282 Sec. 11: an appeal does not suspend collection, but when collection may jeopardize the interest of the government and/or the taxpayer, the CTA may suspend it at any stage and require a deposit or surety bond of not more than double the amount.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 11

q: While a taxpayer's appeal of a P50 million assessment was pending in the CTA, the BIR issued a warrant of garnishment against its bank accounts, threatening to stop its operations. The taxpayer asked the CTA to suspend collection. What may the CTA do?

alac.answer: The CTA may suspend the collection if it finds that collection may jeopardize the interest of the taxpayer or the government, and may require a deposit or bond.
alac.basis: Section 11 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that no appeal taken to the CTA shall suspend the payment, levy, distraint, or sale of any property of the taxpayer, provided that when in the opinion of the Court the collection may jeopardize the interest of the government and/or the taxpayer, the Court at any stage of the proceeding may suspend the collection and require the taxpayer either to deposit the amount claimed or to file a surety bond for not more than double the amount.
alac.application: Here, garnishing all of the taxpayer's bank accounts while the appeal is pending may stop its operations and render the appeal useless, which jeopardizes the taxpayer's interest. The CTA may therefore suspend collection, conditioned on a deposit or a surety bond.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CTA may issue a suspension of collection upon the taxpayer's posting of a cash deposit or a surety bond not exceeding double the amount, unless the circumstances justify dispensing with the bond.

keyPoints: Appeal does not suspend collection as a rule (Sec. 11)
CTA may suspend collection if it jeopardizes interests
Deposit or surety bond of not more than double the amount
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 11

q: Under Section 218 of the NIRC, which court may issue an injunction to restrain the collection of national internal revenue taxes?
choices: No court; but the CTA may suspend collection under its charter
hints: This flows from the lifeblood doctrine.
Suspension by the CTA is a statutory exception.
why: NIRC Sec. 218: no court shall have authority to grant an injunction to restrain collection of national internal revenue taxes; the CTA's power to suspend collection under RA 1125, Sec. 11, as amended, is the exception.
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 218; RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 11

q: A taxpayer filed a petition in the RTC asking it to stop the BIR from enforcing a warrant of levy for unpaid income taxes, alleging that the levy would ruin its business. The RTC issued a TRO. Was the TRO proper?

alac.answer: No, the RTC's TRO was improper.
alac.basis: Section 218 of the NIRC provides that no court shall have the authority to grant an injunction to restrain the collection of any national internal revenue tax, fee or charge imposed by the Code. The only exception is the power of the CTA under Section 11 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, to suspend collection when it may jeopardize the interest of the government or the taxpayer, upon a deposit or bond.
alac.application: Here, the RTC restrained the collection of national internal revenue taxes through a TRO, which it has no authority to issue. The taxpayer's remedy is to pursue its protest and appeal to the CTA, and to seek a suspension of collection from the CTA.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the TRO should be lifted.

keyPoints: No injunction to restrain collection of national taxes (Sec. 218)
Exception: CTA's power to suspend collection (RA 1125, Sec. 11)
Remedy lies with the CTA
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 218; RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 11

q: Criminal actions for violations of the NIRC are instituted:
choices: In the name of the Government, with the approval of the Commissioner, and prosecuted through the DOJ prosecutors (and BIR legal officers)
hints: Sec. 220 requires the CIR's approval.
Jurisdiction follows the P1 million threshold.
why: NIRC Sec. 220: criminal actions are brought in the name of the Government, conducted by BIR legal officers, and filed with the CIR's approval; the complaint is filed with the DOJ for preliminary investigation, and the information is filed with the CTA or the regular courts depending on the amount (RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)).
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 220; RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)

q: A disgruntled former employee filed a criminal complaint for tax evasion against his ex-employer directly with the prosecutor, without any BIR involvement or the CIR's approval. The prosecutor filed an information in court. Is the criminal action properly instituted?

alac.answer: No, the criminal action is not properly instituted without the Commissioner's approval.
alac.basis: Section 220 of the NIRC provides that civil and criminal actions instituted on behalf of the government under the Code shall be brought in the name of the Government of the Philippines and conducted by legal officers of the BIR, and that no civil or criminal action for the recovery of taxes or the enforcement of any fine, penalty or forfeiture under the Code shall be filed in court without the approval of the Commissioner.
alac.application: Here, the complaint was filed by a private person directly with the prosecutor, and the information was filed in court without the Commissioner's approval. The requirement of the Commissioner's approval was not met.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the information may be quashed, without prejudice to the BIR's own investigation and the filing of a case with the Commissioner's approval.

keyPoints: Criminal actions in the name of the Government (Sec. 220)
Commissioner's approval required
Private complainant may report, but the BIR controls the case
cite: National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (NIRC), as amended, Sec. 220

q: Under Section 7(b) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, in tax criminal cases, the corresponding civil action for the recovery of taxes and penalties:
choices: Is filed with the BIR only
Is deemed simultaneously instituted with the criminal action and jointly determined in the same proceeding, and no right to reserve it separately is recognized
hints: The civil action is deemed included.
Reservation of a separate civil action is not allowed.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 7(b): the criminal action and the corresponding civil action for the recovery of taxes and penalties shall at all times be simultaneously instituted with and jointly determined in the same proceeding, the filing of the criminal action being deemed to carry with it the filing of the civil action, and no right to reserve the filing of a separate civil action shall be recognized.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)

q: In a criminal case for tax evasion involving P10 million filed with the CTA, the government moved to reserve the filing of a separate civil action to collect the taxes. Should the CTA grant the reservation?

alac.answer: No, the reservation should be denied.
alac.basis: Section 7(b) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that, any provision of law or the Rules of Court to the contrary notwithstanding, the criminal action and the corresponding civil action for the recovery of civil liability for taxes and penalties shall at all times be simultaneously instituted with, and jointly determined in the same proceeding by the CTA, the filing of the criminal action being deemed to necessarily carry with it the filing of the civil action, and no right to reserve the filing of such civil action separately from the criminal action shall be recognized.
alac.application: Here, the criminal case involves P10 million, within the CTA's original jurisdiction. The civil action for the taxes was deemed filed with the criminal case, and the law does not recognize any reservation of a separate civil action.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CTA should deny the reservation and determine the civil liability for the taxes together with the criminal case.

keyPoints: Civil action deemed instituted with the criminal action (Sec. 7(b))
Jointly determined in the same proceeding
No reservation of a separate civil action
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)

q: In a tax criminal case decided by a regular trial court, the period to appeal the judgment is:
choices: 15 days from promulgation or notice of the judgment, under the Rules of Criminal Procedure
hints: Appeal from the RTC goes to the CTA.
The Revised Rules of the CTA follow Rule 122.
why: Appeals in tax criminal cases follow Rule 122 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure and the Revised Rules of the CTA (A.M. No. 05-11-07-CTA): a notice of appeal within 15 days from promulgation or notice of the judgment; appeals from RTC decisions in such cases go to the CTA (RA 9282, Sec. 7(b)).
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b); Revised Rules of the Court of Tax Appeals (A.M. No. 05-11-07-CTA)

q: An RTC convicted an accused in a tax criminal case involving P600,000 in taxes. The accused filed a notice of appeal with the Court of Appeals on the 25th day from promulgation. Is the appeal properly taken?

alac.answer: No; the appeal was filed late and with the wrong court.
alac.basis: Section 7(b) of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that tax criminal cases where the principal amount is less than P1 million are tried by the regular courts, and that the jurisdiction of the CTA over them is appellate. Under Rule 122 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, applied in the Revised Rules of the CTA, an appeal must be taken within fifteen days from promulgation or notice of the judgment.
alac.application: Here, the case involved P600,000, so the RTC had original jurisdiction, but the appeal lies with the CTA, not the Court of Appeals. The notice of appeal was also filed on the 25th day, beyond the fifteen-day period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the appeal is improper, and the judgment of conviction has become final.

keyPoints: Below P1 million: regular courts, CTA appellate (Sec. 7(b))
Appeal within 15 days (Rule 122)
Appeal to the CTA, not the CA
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 7(b); Revised Rules of the Court of Tax Appeals (A.M. No. 05-11-07-CTA)

q: Under Section 18 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, a party adversely affected by a decision of a CTA Division may file a petition for review with the CTA en banc:
choices: Directly with the Supreme Court instead
After filing a timely motion for reconsideration or new trial with the Division
Only with the Secretary of Justice
hints: A motion for reconsideration is a condition.
Under the Revised Rules of the CTA, the petition is filed within 15 days from receipt of the resolution.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 18: a party adversely affected by a decision of a CTA Division, on a motion for reconsideration or new trial, may file a petition for review with the CTA en banc; under the Revised Rules of the CTA, within 15 days from receipt of the resolution, extendible for 15 days.
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 18; Revised Rules of the Court of Tax Appeals (A.M. No. 05-11-07-CTA)

q: A CTA Division ruled against the CIR in a refund case. The CIR, without first filing a motion for reconsideration with the Division, filed a petition for review with the CTA en banc. Should the en banc entertain it?

alac.answer: No, the petition should be dismissed for failure to first file a motion for reconsideration with the Division.
alac.basis: Section 18 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that a party adversely affected by a resolution of a Division of the CTA on a motion for reconsideration or new trial may file a petition for review with the CTA en banc. Under the Revised Rules of the Court of Tax Appeals, a prior motion for reconsideration or new trial with the Division is a condition for an appeal to the en banc.
alac.application: Here, the CIR went directly to the CTA en banc without first moving for reconsideration of the Division's decision. It skipped a required step.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the en banc should dismiss the petition.

keyPoints: Petition for review with the CTA en banc (Sec. 18)
Prior motion for reconsideration or new trial with the Division required
Failure is fatal
cite: RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, Sec. 18; Revised Rules of the Court of Tax Appeals (A.M. No. 05-11-07-CTA)

q: Under Section 19 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, a decision of the CTA en banc may be reviewed by the Supreme Court through:
choices: Petition for certiorari under Rule 65 only
A verified petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45
Motion to the Secretary of Finance
hints: Only questions of law are generally raised under Rule 45.
The period is 15 days from notice.
why: RA 9282 Sec. 19: a party adversely affected by a decision or ruling of the CTA en banc may file with the Supreme Court a verified petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, generally raising only questions of law, within 15 days from notice.

q: After losing in the CTA en banc, a taxpayer filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the Court of Appeals, asking it to re-examine the evidence on its sales. Is this the correct remedy?

alac.answer: No; the correct remedy is a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 with the Supreme Court, generally on questions of law.
alac.basis: Section 19 of RA 1125, as amended by RA 9282, provides that a party adversely affected by a decision or ruling of the CTA en banc may file with the Supreme Court a verified petition for review on certiorari pursuant to Rule 45 of the Rules of Civil Procedure. The CTA is of the same level as the Court of Appeals, so the CA has no jurisdiction to review its decisions, and a Rule 45 petition generally raises only questions of law, since the CTA's factual findings are respected.
alac.application: Here, the taxpayer went to the Court of Appeals under Rule 65 and asked it to re-weigh the evidence on its sales. The CA cannot review CTA en banc decisions, and the proper remedy is a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court, which generally will not re-examine factual findings.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the CA petition should be dismissed; the taxpayer should have filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court within the period.
